We probably should move, not because housing is unaffordable, in fact a massive home is $200k. Due to currency depreciation a home bought for $200k in 2010 is now only $80k. So housing is cheaper, but is a function of a dysfunctional economy.

However, many friends have moved to other countries because of a weak economy over past 2 decades. But to move it means we need to leave family behind, especially older parents. It is very hard to leave behind family connections, so we stay.

I guess you just have to be happy with your choices, because everything is a choice.

As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

To keep things non-promotional, please use a real name or nickname(not Blogger @ My Blog Name)

The most useful comments are those written with the goal of learning from or helping out other readers – after reading the whole article and all the earlier comments. Complaints and insults generally won’t make the cut here, but by all means write them on your own blog!

#8777. JASON AVELAR AND GARRETT BEAL SHARE THE STORY OF PRESCOTT JUNIOR HIGH’S LEGACY OF PHYSICAL EDUCATION EXCELLENCE

President Donald Trump announced the re-establishment and restoration of the Presidential Fitness Test on July 31, 2025, when he signed an Executive Order revitalizing the test along with the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition. Since then, the Trump administration also announced the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, a competition which invites “schools, districts, and youth-serving organizations to design and execute creative, repeatable models that inspire student participation, teamwork, and enthusiasm for the Presidential Fitness Test (PFT).”

One school that could serve as an example for others to follow and may be a top contender should they enter that challenge would be Prescott Junior High School in Modesto, California. The school overall has a great reputation, but it is best known for their P.E. program. Current teachers Jason Avelar and Garrett Beal are two of the teachers for this program, but its legacy as a fitness-focused juggernaut goes back nearly a half-century.

Beal, who also served as a police officer for a period of his life, played sports as a kid but credited a high school wrestling coach for introducing him to the weight room.

“It was the first sport where I saw that being strong helped,” he said. “I fell in love even more with fitness than wrestling.”

Avelar was bitten by the iron bug while playing football in his high school days but also found he had natural leadership skills as a linebacker. His coaches confirmed this and could have played a role in him becoming a gym teacher.

“I had a few coaches and teachers pull me aside and said, ‘Hey, I think you’d be a great teacher.’”

Both Beal and Alevar are reminded often about the history they are a part of. Modeled closely after the La Sierra High School Physical Education Program (the famous 1960s President’s Council on Physical Fitness model) Prescott’s program has challenged junior high students for decades using a high-standard and military-inspired structure.

In 1973, then Prescott P.E. teacher Mark Wilson saw a demonstration of a high-intensity, physical fitness-based curriculum. Wilson was inspired by the concept and used his own version on his students, challenging them to make fitness a priority at an early age.

There is a color and points based system to help gauge the students’ progress and motivate them to work harder. All students start with zero points and white trunks, and there are 20 different fitness tests. Each test offers one, two, or four points for their performances. Once a student achieves 60 points, they earn red trunks. However, the scoring goes back to zero because they are at a new level with harder challenges. Once they work back up to 60 points, they then earn blue trunks.

“The tests at that point get very challenging,” Avelar said. There are also gold and purple trunks for those students that do very well in the program. Prescott even has a P.E. Hall of Fame, where students can be recognized. Avelar acknowledged one student who even cleared the purple trunk scoring early, meaning they had to create a new level just for her.

“We decided on custom trunks. Once you pass purple, you get to pick your own.”

The bars may be seen as super high for some, but Avelar and Beal share that either students rise to the occasion and reach it, or they get closer than they may have had there not been that high bar in the first place.

The results speak for themselves. One student ran two miles in 12 minutes, 27 seconds. Another performed over 6,000 continuous sit-ups, and multiple students have reportedly performed over 1,000 unbroken pushups. The Prescott program has had a generational impact in Modesto.

Beal said, “I wear my Prescott shirt anywhere around town, and people stop to talk to me about when they went there.” He even met one man at a book club, and he recognized the last name on their Hall of Fame wall.

Other teachers at Prescott were also students there, and both Beal and Avelar confirmed that they strive to be the best examples possible by making their wellness a priority. They also said that even though the high school P.E. programs may not have as intense of programs, the students who went to Prescott continue their fitness journeys after they move on. Others may take the school for granted but realize what they were a part of later on.

Avelar said, “As they leave, they realize ‘Oh crap, this is a super special place.’”

Both teachers take great pride in not only what they are a part of but having added their own chapters to the Prescott story. They are reminded of how important their work is every day, and they definitely don’t take the positions they are in for granted.

Avelar stated. “The fulfillment I get from showing up to school every day and seeing kids reach their goals, push themselves, do things they’ve never done before, and seeing the excitement on their faces is why I do it.”

Beal added, “This is such a special place to be,”

There is no official word on how many schools will enter the Presidential Fitness School Innovation Challenge, but both Avelar and Beal were pleased that the Presidential Fitness Test has been reinstated, and they hope that it can serve as a catalyst for other P.E. programs to do more to help their students embrace fitness, pushing themselves, and taking on great challenges. As they have seen first hand, the impact goes beyond the school walls and can last for many years to come.

To learn more about the PFT or the School Innovation Challenge, go to fitness.gov.

You can follow the Prescott program on Instagram @prescott_standard and Beal and Alevar on LinkedIn.

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

#8773. World Anti-Doping Agency’s Latest Banned List Sends a Warning to Athletes Looking for ‘Loopholes’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

There is a certain kind of athlete who treats the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list like a treasure map. He reads it, finds something that isn’t printed there, and figures he’s discovered a loophole. The molecule has a name that sounds like a Wi-Fi password, the vial says “research use only,” and some guy with a podcast swears it repairs tendons, melts fat, or turns you into a gazelle. Perfect. What could possibly go wrong?

Well, WADA just made that little game harder. Its 2027 Prohibited List, which takes effect Jan. 1, now explicitly mentions peptides in the category for non-approved substances. The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency put out an advisory explaining the change and warning athletes not to assume an experimental peptide is legal simply because its particular alphabet soup isn’t spelled out on the list. That’s a useful distinction, because the peptide business has become a sprawling mess of legitimate medicine, promising research, questionable claims, and little bottles of who-the-hell-knows-what.

Before anybody starts screaming that WADA banned every peptide on earth, it didn’t. Peptides are chains of amino acids, and some are established medicines. Insulin is a peptide. The relevant category, called S0, covers pharmacological substances without approval for human therapeutic use by a government health authority anywhere in the world, provided they aren’t already covered by another prohibited class. Some peptides fall into other categories. The word “peptides” appearing in S0 is a clarification, not a declaration that every peptide drug is forbidden.

The important point is that experimental substances weren’t necessarily fair game yesterday. BPC-157, for example, was already prohibited under the rules for non-approved substances. Others, including certain growth-hormone-related compounds, are covered elsewhere. What changed is the language, making it even harder to pretend that an unlisted research chemical gets a free pass. And if you compete in a tested sport, “I couldn’t find it on Google” ranks right up there with road rage. No one is gonna buy it.

There are some other interesting additions as well. WADA names two experimental metabolic modulators, SLU-PP-332 and SLU-PP-915, as examples in its hormone and metabolic modulators category. The list also adds examples of diuretics and masking agents, including eplerenone and finerenone, drugs that have perfectly legitimate medical uses. That’s another reality athletes forget: the prohibited list isn’t just a catalog of things somebody invented to cheat. It can include ordinary prescription medications, depending on the drug and circumstances.

Meanwhile, semaglutide and tirzepatide, the active ingredients in two widely used families of weight-loss and diabetes treatments, remain on WADA’s monitoring program for 2027. Monitoring is not banning. WADA is collecting information about their use in sport; it has not put them on the prohibited list. The same distinction matters with caffeine, which is monitored in competition but not prohibited. Which makes me feel good that the people making the rules recognize a difference between watching something and convicting it.

While they were at it, they also tuned up the cannabis language. WADA clarified that psychoactive THC-related cannabinoids, including certain synthetic and semi-synthetic versions, are prohibited in competition. CBD itself isn’t prohibited, but a CBD product containing undeclared THC can still create a problem. Meaning, you run the risk of failing a drug test.

It doesn’t matter if you’re an Olympian, a fighter, a weightlifter, or some local competitor. Under anti-doping rules, athletes are responsible for what’s in their bodies. What’s missing off a label is not an alibi. Neither is a coach or a doctor. You’re on your own. So play the game wisely.

I am 100% for researching new performance drugs. That’s how some useful things eventually get discovered. But research is not approval, and a promising animal study is not proof in humans. None of that really matters to many athletes because they usually rely on anecdotal evidence. They will do it anyway—if they think it works and can find a way of not getting caught. Which, for the most part, in my view of things, they do. But if your competitive career matters to you, you need to be very careful, as peptides create a very broad gray area. Make sure you check the actual status of the substance before you put it in your body—and remember, just because WADA has banned it doesn’t mean that there’s a test for it. January isn’t far away, and WADA is making one thing abundantly clear: They’re always a step behind. I guess it never occurs to them to switch hats and discover the new stuff before we do.

#8769. Ilona Maher Now Looking to Take Rugby—and Girls’ Fitness—to the Next Level

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

During the 2024 Paris Olympics, USA women’s team rugby player Ilona Maher suddenly became a household name.

“I think for some people when they get famous, maybe it changes who they are and who they believe themselves to be,” Maher tells Muscle & Fitness. “I just never found that to be me.I think I’m kind of a similar person I was before the Paris Olympics.”

The bronze-medal winner posed on the cover of Sports Illustrated shortly after the games wrapped. From there, Maher went on to compete on Dancing with the Stars, launch a successful podcast, and secure major partnerships with brands like Maybelline New York, Adidas and Burn Boot Camp.

Although it seems like all eyes are on Maher, very few of her fans are watching her while she’s on the field that made her a celebrity.

“Honestly, it doesn’t frustrate me because we don’t have enough places for them to watch rugby,” Maher says. “So I would tell you to watch rugby. I could tell you there’s games on this weekend, but it’s not like you tune into one game, then I’ll keep watching that team.”

Despite the lack of eyeballs on the game, much like Caitlin Clark in the WNBA, Maher is credited for helping put the game back on the map and even boosting ticket sales.

“That’s where it’s hard for me is that there’s really not a lot of opportunities to watch the game,” Maher explains. “And when they want to watch me play—a lot of people would love to watch me play, but I play in places like South Africa and then I go to Perth. So if you want to wake up at 4 in the morning to watch me play the first two minutes of a game…”

Although Maher admits it’s a hard pill to swallow, she doesn’t let it discourage her and remains hopeful for the future of the sport.

“It’s a very tough thing in that I want to get more people in. I think more people should be in, but there we need more opportunities or need more things for [fans], games and in terms for them to be able to watch that are on home soil, too.”

The San Diego resident currently has her sights set on the 2028 L.A. summer games so all of her other projects get planned around her training for Team USA.

“We have meetings throughout the day and rehab and stretching to ramp the body up and whatnot,” explains Maher. “I have to do whatever timing my team says. I’m not an individual athlete that can build my life around my podcast. I have to build the podcast and everything else around my training life, I have to be in the gym at 8 a.m. with all the girls. It’s not worth it to miss a day of training when maybe something else will come up, because I do think I’m a team athlete through and through.”

Despite knowing her obligations to her teammates come first, Maher understands there’s a balance, especially to keep people intrigued in the sport for the upcoming olympic games.

“If my girls are grinding, I want to be out there grinding with them and not just taking the easy road,” Maher says. “But it is important for me to also focus on things like the podcasts or speaking, because that’s how I financially live the life I do.”

Maher admits she’s become so popular that she’s had to pass on some things to prioritize her love of the game.

“I have to say no to a lot of opportunities,” Maher says. “I will get invited to this cool event and I just have to pick my battles.”

Maher admits her newfound fame has created a “pretty hefty schedule,” her physical training remains her top priority. Her training schedule includes two daily on-field sessions along with a gym workout that can include speed and skills work, and up to about 20,000 steps of running. She also adds four days fo weightroom work, focusing explosive movements. The days she’s out of the gym, Maher is recovering and prepping to repeat the same schedule the following week.

The athlete says she thrives on pushing her limits in the weight room, especially with squats and bench presses.

“I like the ones where you really get to like to test yourself and see how much more you can do,” Maher says.

Despite being a professional athlete, Maher admits she still has her own personal wins in the gym.

“I do love dumb bell incline bench press,” explains Maher. “Where you do a weight and then you’re like, ‘I think I can do a little bit more weight!’ and you put a little more weight and you did and you’re like, ‘OK, I can do a little more weight. Those are the moments where I really love being in the gym”.

Off the field, Maher knows girls everywhere are looking up to her for guidance and empowerment, which is why she partnered with Burn Boot Camp to spread the message about their 45-minute high-intensity fitness classes.

“I just watched it and the energy and the way that these women came to this class, so excited to be there,” says Maher. They were high-fiving each other and they were getting stronger and it was the sort of community that I’m trying to foster and I think create, and that’s why I decided to work with this brand. Because I have so many girls who message me saying, ‘I wanna get strong. I wanna be strong like you. I just don’t know where to start and I’m intimidated by the gym.’

#8765. Science Has Zeroed in on Why Lifters Need Cardio for Heart Health

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Every gym (real gym) has a dude like this—we used to call them “fire plugs” (if you’re not from New York, that means fire hydrant). He has arms like sewer pipes, a chest like a gun safe, zero degrees of V-taper, and he’d probably be proud of the fact that he has a squat rack in his living room in case he needs some extra sets—your basic Midwestern corn-fed Jethro type. The exact guy you would never imagine seeing on a treadmill.

Cardio? That’s what people do when they don’t have huge muscles to worry about. Besides, he can see his abs (ab, actually, but it’s like a rock). What more evidence of health could anybody possibly need?

That depends on how long Jethro wants to live. A study recently published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise looked at 562,234 adults who had undergone clinical treadmill testing. Researchers wanted to know whether measuring cardiorespiratory fitness improved predictions of who would die over the following decade, beyond the usual suspects: age, sex, high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol problems, and smoking. The answer was yes. Not because the treadmill possesses magical cognitive powers, but because how much work your heart and lungs can support tells doctors something the other numbers don’t.

The researchers measured peak exercise capacity in Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET). It’s a way of expressing how much energy a physical activity demands relative to rest. In the study, the bottom fifth of fitness fell below five METs. After adjusting for traditional risk factors, the estimated ten-year mortality risk in that least-fit group was 32.9 percent, compared with 13.4 percent among the fitter participants. That’s a considerable difference, even allowing for the fact that these were people referred for clinical exercise tests, not a random cross-section of every healthy person walking around America.

Another number worth understanding correctly is that each additional MET of measured fitness was associated with a 16 percent lower hazard of death over follow-up. Notice I said associated. Not caused. The researchers did not take half a million people, put some on treadmills, leave the others on the couch, and wait ten years to see who was still kicking. This was an observational analysis. Healthier people may be able to exercise harder because they’re healthier in the first place. The study accounted for several major risk factors, but it cannot eliminate every possible explanation.

Nor did adding fitness transform mortality prediction into a crystal ball. The model’s discrimination score improved from 0.662 to 0.682 when cardiorespiratory fitness was included. That’s statistically meaningful and potentially useful, but modest. The headline isn’t that doctors can now tell you the day you’ll die by watching you jog, but rather that a basic measure of physical capacity deserves a seat at the table alongside blood pressure and the rest of the measurable health markers.

What I find fascinating is the cultural blind spot this exposes. Bodybuilders understand that muscle matters, as do strength, bone loading, glucose regulation, mobility, and the ability to get yourself up off the toilet when you’re eighty—all excellent reasons to keep lifting. Somewhere along the line, a segment of the iron community decided that cardio was bad. It was either an inconvenience or an enemy that ate muscle, or both. A lot of old-school, Arnold-era bodybuilders didn’t do cardio. Then suddenly the Life Cycle was invented, and a lot of us felt good about adding endurance training to our mix, mainly because of the massive calves and quads we started to see on Olympic cyclists. So, maybe there’s something to this? Blasphemy!

Until you consider your heart and your potential lifespan, with or without cardio and with or without muscle.

Of course, if you’re a bodybuilder, you’re going to take an extremist position. But you don’t have to become a distance runner. In fact, if your knees, hips, or general disposition object to running, there are bicycles, rowing machines, swimming pools, incline walks, and any number of ways to get your breathing up without pounding pavement. The practical target isn’t to chase a laboratory number you saw in an article. It’s to build enough aerobic capacity that ordinary life doesn’t feel like a stress test. Start where you are, progress gradually, and if you have symptoms or known heart disease, get medical guidance before going all out.

I still think a man should be strong. But if he’s strong enough to deadlift a Buick and gets gassed carrying groceries up one flight of stairs, we might have overlooked something. For the slight handful of you who compete at a very high level, doing cardio is etched into your coach’s DNA at this point. You have no choice. Except to keep doing it after the show is over. The rest of you, do cardio! Times have changed, technology has changed, and research has accumulated. Adding these data to the mountain of evidence thus collected on the topic, the overall consensus, if your desire is longevity, is simple: the lighter, stronger, leaner, and more cardiovascularly fit you are, the longer you get to bother everyone.

#8761. 5 Mobility Moves to Improve Your Bulgarian Split Squats

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

The Bulgarian split squat is the exercise almost all lifters love to hate. Still, you cannot deny its benefits, including increased quad and glute strength and size and reduced strength imbalances, which can improve bilateral squats.

But it has a funny way of humbling those who perform it because it demands more than strength. It requires hip mobility, ankle dorsiflexion, pelvic control, and single-leg stability.

If one of those is off, let’s hope you’re not on camera.

Here, I’ll cover common BSS performance issues and five mobility exercises to help you get the most out of the most dreaded exercise in gym history.

Before blaming the Bulgarian split squat for all your woes, let’s test whether it’s a mobility issue.

The goal isn’t a perfect-looking rep but finding any performance limitations that are holding back your gains. But before adding mobility drills, let’s see if it’s a setup issue.

Not every Bulgarian split squat problem requires another corrective drill. Before blaming tight hips and reaching for the foam roller, a few small adjustments could make a big difference.

About to perform Bulgarian split squats? Here’s what your body needs to bring to that first set.

A well-performed Bulgarian split squat requires hip and ankle mobility and stability everywhere else. Mobility gets you into position, but strength and stability let you own it.

5 MOBILITY MOVES TO OWN THE BOTTOM POSITION OF YOUR BULGARIAN SPLIT SQUAT

If the adjustments above cleaned up your performance issues, great, you’re good to go. If not, the five mobility exercises below are exactly what you need.

The Bulgarian split squat may be an up-and-down exercise, but your hips must also control side-to-side movement to keep your pelvis and knees stable. That’s where the Lateral Lunge to Box earns its keep. It improves adductor mobility and builds hip strength and control, allowing you to reach the bottom without issues.

Why Lifters Need It: The lateral lunge to box trains the adductors through a lengthened position while developing the hip strength and mobility needed to resist excessive lateral shifting.

Programming Suggestions: You can perform this unloaded as a warm-up for 10 reps per side, or load it up as an accessory movement for your squats and deadlifts for 2-4 sets of 8-15 reps per side.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/TML8Vqy-ACQ

If your rear hip flexors and quads are tight, it’s hard to get to the bottom without arching your lower back. The Couch Stretch targets the hip flexors and quads that can restrict the rear leg.

Why Lifters Need It: The rectus femoris is unique among the quadriceps because it crosses both the hip and knee joints. If it’s restricted, you may feel excessive pulling in the front of your thigh, arch your lower back, or shorten your range of motion to avoid discomfort. The Couch Stretch can restore length to the rectus femoris and the quads.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 30-60 seconds per side as part of your warmup.

If you struggle to get your knees over your toes, your heel may lift, your balance may suffer, and your knee may have difficulty moving forward. The Weighted Ankle Rocker helps you build that missing range without any mobility circus tricks.

Why Lifters Need It: During the Bulgarian split squat, your front ankle moves into dorsiflexion as your knee travels forward over it. Sufficient dorsiflexion lets you distribute pressure evenly across your foot as you lower to the bottom position.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 8 reps per side as part of your warm-up.

4. Front-Foot Elevated Split Squat With Pause

The front-foot-elevated split squat made the list because it promotes deeper hip and knee flexion. You might be able to get into a deep split squat, but if you bounce out of the bottom or lack the strength to hold it, this variation builds the mobility and strength needed for the BSS bottom position.

Why Lifters Need It: If you lack strength at the end of the range of motion, you may rush the eccentric or rely too much on the rear leg. Elevating the front foot lets you practice a deeper split squat position, while adding a pause builds strength there.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 6 reps per side with a three-second pause at the bottom as part of your warmup.

5. Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Mobilization With Overhead Reach

There are other hip flexors besides the rectus femoris needed for the Bulgarian split squat. Your iliopsoas, the other hip flexor, also affects how your rear hip extends. This mobility drill strengthens hip extension while maintaining pelvic stability and improves iliopsoas length. The overhead reach and side bend add extra range and intensity.

Why Lifters Need It: When your trailing hip lacks full extension due to short hip flexors, you may compensate by arching your lower back or tipping your pelvis forward as you descend. A few sets of these will have your hips primed for the BSS, even if you are not.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 8 reaches per side, pausing for three seconds in the stretched position.

The Bulgarian split squat is tough enough without performance issues fighting you on every rep. The gains happen when you reach the bottom, when the muscles are under a loaded stretch. If getting there is a problem, fixing the setup and mobility issues will help.

Mobility gets you to the bottom, and strength and stability get you out. Master both, and this dreaded exercise becomes one of your best tools for building stronger legs.

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

There were many reasons to be excited about the 2026 Olympia Weekend in Las Vegas, NV, but one that got a lot of attention was the new Fit Model Olympia category. This inaugural show meant that every athlete who graced the stage was a part of bodybuilding history.

One of those competitors was Svetlana Fedkina, and she feels that fate and hard work were what led her to that moment.

“I remember when (IFBB Pro League Vice President) Tyler Manion announced the new Fit Model division in December 2024. My first thought was, ‘This is my chance. Maybe this is my path to the Olympia.’ Of course, I didn’t know that I would actually make it there, but for the first time in a long time, I saw a division where I felt I could truly show who I am as an athlete.”

Fedkina said that competing in bodybuilding shows felt like a natural continuation of her sports life, which included ballet for most of her childhood. She discovered the Bikini division in 2013 and could see herself competing in those shows.

“That’s really why I fell in love with bodybuilding. For me, it brings together everything I love: sports, discipline, constant self-improvement, aesthetics, and the opportunity to perform and express myself on stage.”

Fedkina enjoys competing but also acknowledges a higher purpose: inspiring people to improve themselves and make changes for the better.

She said, “I want people, especially women, to see that being strong and healthy can also be feminine and beautiful. If my own journey can inspire someone to become a better version of themselves, that means a lot to me.”

When the Fit Model category was announced, Fedkina saw an opportunity to train and showcase her ultimate form as an athlete. When she first started competing in Bikini, Ashley Kaltwasser was the reigning Olympia champion. Her look from back then was acknowledged by the IFBB Pro League as the inspiration and standard for this new division.

Call it inspiration or divine intervention, but Fedkina felt this was more than a new category for her to enter. The years of pursuing a pro card in her previous class may have seemed like failure at the moment, but now she feels they were stepping stones to this point.

“I also had this strong feeling that everything I had been through in the sport was somehow preparing me for this opportunity.”

She earned that coveted pro card in May 2026 at the Junior USA event. She made her pro debut one month later at the St. Pete Pro, taking eighth place. Then came Tampa. In only her second pro show, Fedkina not only took first place but earned an Olympia qualification as a result. That qualification culminated in a sixth-place finish at the inaugural Fit Model Olympia.

“Being part of the first-ever Fit Model Olympia was incredibly special to me,” she said. “It was a historic moment not only for our division, but for the sport of professional bodybuilding as Fit Model made its debut on the Olympia stage. I’m very proud that my name will always be part of that history.”

Regardless of the result, Fedkina already made her own history by becoming the first Slavic athlete to qualify for the Fit Model Olympia. While she is proud of that, she also understands it came thanks in part to timing and opportunity. She’s thinking more about what she can do with that accolade going forward, including inspiring other athletes to follow suit and join her on the Olympia stage.

“I hope it can inspire other women from that part of the world as well. Sometimes your opportunity doesn’t come when you expect it to. You just have to keep going long enough to be ready when it finally does.”

After starting 2026 as an amateur, she made her Olympia debut and left as one of the top six in her category, making her a potential contender to watch in 2027. As is the case with many world-class athletes, Fedkina has already set her sights on what is ahead and plans on finishing better than sixth if she makes it back onto the Olympia stage.

“That result gave me two things at the same time: confirmation that we did a lot right, and even more motivation because I can clearly see that there is still room to grow. It showed me that I can compete at this level, and it made me even more excited to see how far I can take this.”

Fedkina shared a lower body workout that she used during her Olympia prep. She feels that even though the standards are different from Wellness or Bikini, you still need to prepare for hard work when you go into the gym. She emphasized her setup of the Bulgarian split squats if this is a harder area for a lifter to develop.

“It is basically the only exercise I do all week that significantly involves my quads. Over time, I’ve developed a specific setup and technique, including using a resistance band around my working knee, that helps me shift most of the work toward my glutes.”

Fedkina typically rests for 1.5-2 minutes but will take as much as five for more difficult sets.

Replays of the 2026 Olympia can be seen at olympiaproductions.com. You can follow Fedkina on Instagram @sweetlana_ifbbpro.

#8751. How Yonatan Katz Cracked the Boulder Nobody Could Solve at the World Climbing Series

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Climbing is what happens when you take a gym rat’s obsession with grip strength, remove the floor, and let gravity do its thing. There’s no bench to lie on, no belt to tighten, and no place to hide a weak link. You have to get your body up a wall using holds that sometimes look so bleak the edge of a credit card looks like it might offer more purchase. And if you screw up, you better hope your rope is knotted correctly.

That was on full display at the World Climbing Series bouldering finale in Salt Lake City, October 16-18. In the men’s final, Israel’s Yonatan Katz won gold on only his second start in the senior international series. He went into the final problem behind Britain’s Maximillian Milne and came out the winner after pulling off a move nobody else in the final had managed.

Here’s how it happened. The last boulder was a nasty coordination problem. Before Katz stepped up, the other finalists who had attempted it hadn’t even reached the scoring zone, a designated hold partway up the route. On his fourth try, Katz got past the zone and reached the top. He finished with 69.7 points. Milne couldn’t answer on his turn and took silver with 59.7. Japan’s Rei Kawamata was third with 54.2. For a sport that looks, to outsiders, like a bunch of people climbing a wall, there was a hell of a lot of drama hanging off those holds.

The women’s final the next day had its own story. France’s Oriane Bertone won with 84.6 points after being the only finalist to complete the first boulder. Britain’s Erin McNeice finished second with 69.7, barely ahead of Japan’s Mao Nakamura at 69.6. McNeice didn’t win that night, but she won the season-long Boulder title. She’d opened the series in 11th place and followed it with a gold and four silvers.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Sorato Anraku had already locked up the men’s overall championship after winning five of the six bouldering events. Then he failed to advance from qualification in Salt Lake City. Even the guy who dominated the season can get humbled by a fresh set of plastic holds. If bodybuilding judges replaced their comparison rounds with problems that changed every week, we’d see a few interesting faces backstage.

Bouldering is done on relatively short walls with thick mats instead of ropes. The athlete has to solve a sequence of moves, reach designated holds, and control the top. Strength matters, obviously. So does the ability to position your hips, push through your feet, generate momentum, and decide what to do before your forearms turn into concrete. Some moves are slow and surgical. Others look like a gymnast being thrown into a hardware store. The best climbers aren’t simply pulling themselves upward. They’re figuring out how to make the least-wasteful movement possible under pressure.

There’s a lesson in there for anybody who trains. A giant back and a crushing handshake don’t automatically make you good at something that requires timing, balance, and technical skill. Nor does being smaller make you weak. Climbing exposes the difference between owning strength and knowing how to use it. And if you’re tempted to try it, start with an introductory session, not an advanced overhang and a heroic declaration. A 2026 review of 45 climbing-injury studies found frequent problems involving fingers, hands, shoulders, and ankles. Those little finger pulleys weren’t designed to absorb your entire ego on day one.

I like sports that punish bullshit. Climbing is high on that list. There’s no score for looking intimidating while you chalk your hands, and no bonus for explaining how strong you’d be if the holds were bigger. Katz won because he solved a problem that had stopped the others. McNeice took the season because she kept delivering. The wall doesn’t care about your résumé, your physique, or your excuses. It only cares whether you can get to the top.

#8748. The Ultimate Life Coach

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

To most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

So I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:

I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

See, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:

I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

It’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

As part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and issues, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:

I now realize that things are more like this:

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

So the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

For me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

While the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

People that do ‘hard’ things for long-term reasons, i.e. ‘I exercise to live longer’ or ‘I exercise to be healthy’, do 30% less exercise than people who exercise for the immediate benefits like ‘I want to feel better today!’ or ‘I exercise to feel more energised TODAY’.

I gave this reframing a go for sitting down to write. I changed from ‘I want to write so that in the future I will have a newsletter that serves others and makes me money’ to ‘I want to write because of the state of flow I will feel in the moment and the sense of achievement I will feel TODAY’. Gretchen Rubin talks about ‘obligers’ who can only meet other peoples expectations. This is ~ 40% of humanity and I think this is key to who thrives when retired and who doesn’t. In your work out example I would use focusmate, book an appointment, and then I would have to meet the person on time (online) to do the workout.

Nothing wrong with taking things easy once you’ve “made it” but you bring up a good point around self-actualization. We all (well most maybe) want to feel like we are living our best life, and striving for something, whether a workout routine or starting a business, can do that. I do think it can be dangerous though to listen to people putting up their best game face and saying they run 50 miles a day while being CEO and charity president etc, as everyone is wired differently.

I think FI is wonderful because it enables you to do what you want and contribute your best skills to society. The face that you’ve volunteered and helped with construction projects is great. It’s a lot better than most people who just want to indulge and travel the world while contributing as little as possible to taxes and society.

We do need more people to be citizen voices in politics rather than full-time lobbyists, so people-centered legislation can pass instead of that which benefits the Uber-wealthy and corporations. I hope more early retirees can be advocates of causes important to them and spark change while the rest of us are still at work.

I find myself confused regarding what is actually good for the body. For about a 2 year period, I lifted weights regularly and stuck to a program. I got results and gained some strength but I injured my knees and eventually gave it up. Furthermore, I’ve been following the Blue Zones work by Dan Buettner, and these studies show that the longest lived and healthiest people in the world do not work out in the gym at all, they simply do physical labor naturally (walking up and down steep hills, gardening, etc…). That being said, I wonder if these super muscular gym rats / ultra marathoners are actually living longer and healthier lives. Is there any evidence of this?

There’s always going to be outliers in either direction but I’d say people who go to the gym or do some sort of scheduled routine exercise definitely are in general healthier. Now if you’re juicing or going for PBs all the time then maybe that’s not so healthy but otherwise it’s pretty easy to say that moving more is healthier than moving less. Also the gym is not just

I have wondered about this myself. What is the scientific evidence? Extreme exercise does not seem to increase lifespan/healthspan.

I want to work out today. I don’t feel like it. ^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^ I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

. . . is pure Stoicism, a topic you have touched on before.

That little voice in your head that says “I don’t feel like it” is what the Stoics called “an impression.” You have clearly learned to apply “prosoche” (mindfulness would be a good translation of this Greek word) to interrogate that impression. Then you applied natural wisdom (one of the Stoic virtues) to reach the logical conclusion that surrendering to that impression would not be in your best interest.

There is another Stoic echo in your rediscovered commitment to exercise. The Stoics strongly believed that it was crucial to constantly test oneself, whether that meant fasting, walking barefoot in the now, or undertaking difficult or unpleasant tasks.

So well done! You are proving an apt “prokopton” (one who is making progress to becoming a Stoic sage).

As a retired person I can really relate to this. For me it’s not the lack of desire to do hard things, it’s the easy distracting nature of the phone. I get bored, pull out my phone, then wonder where the last eight hours went.

People with jobs and young kids have to put down the phone to go to work, or take the kids to school. I could spend 100% of my time on YouTube, and my brain will do that if I let it.

My retired quality of life improved immensely when I started keeping my phone and computer in my office out of reach.

Now I get bored, feel uncomfortable, then go and do something. That feeling of boredom and discomfort is critical to making me do the things that actually bring joy to my life.

Boredom is a signal that I have spare energy that should be used for something. Phones alleviate boredom and kill motivation

Little off topic, but what were your final thoughts of Culdesac in Arizona? Would you ever consider moving there? Was there a sense of community and collaboration?

Hey RH, thanks for following along with that. Throughout my stay there, I kept this page updated, and it’s now in its final form with all my thoughts so far: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Summary: there is *some* community forming there, but not as much as I expected going in – they’re still working on building out the neighborhood so it’s a tough chicken-and-egg problem to crack. How do you attract people who really want to hang out with their neighbors rather than just people looking to hide away in their apartments? The Culdesac team are fantastic however, and of course the physical architecture of the place is beautiful. So I think they are doing the right things to build it out.

Glad to hear you’re picking up Extreme Ownership! As someone who is still in his working years, it’s made the way I think about getting work done much better. In software engineering, sometimes shit just goes wrong. Knowing that almost everything can be avoided by us engineers doing a better and robust job has improved the way I work and has made me _less_ stressed, because the work I do is better and more well thought out from the start. Even when something does go wrong, it’s just a learning experience that allows me to avoid those pitfalls in the future.

This book is even better for your social relationships though! Most of the time, you can be the ignition to a better relationship with someone. I’ve seen it many times where relationships you want drift away because neither side initiates social interaction enough with the other. “If they really care, they’d reach out.” Turns out, if you take ownership and reach out, you’ll see them a lot more and be happier as a result. The same thing applies for someone toxic in your life. Tired of this person bringing you down? Take ownership and remove yourself from the equation. (Obviously there are circumstances where this doesn’t apply, but you’ll know it when you see it).

Plus the narration of the audiobook is just great. Jocko has that Seal Team motivational way of speaking that makes you get your shit together!

I was in a similar situation. Thank you for writing this post. I thought everyone else had their act together, so hearing that you had similar challenges made me feel ‘normal’. I also discovered Goggins, and have been using it to do things I know I need to do, but procrastinated on

I have noticed a lot less posts over the past year.. Is this part of of “not doing” what you want to do.. or something else?

Try a HappyLight by Verilux or similar product. Helped me a lot, especially in the winter months.

Thank you for posting this and articulating ideas many are feeling on this blog. I’ve been facing much of this same internal dialog from the perspective of working 20 years at a career I enjoy that pays well. With that job I enjoy I still think about quality of life and wonder about meaning as my children grow older and my spouse and I get closer to financial freedom.

It’s a weird place to be to doubt internally whether I actually want to retire as the feasibility becomes more real. Anyone else feeling the same and concerned not putting myself in the situation explained in the blog is actually easier than having to deal with the procrastination?

Secondly, a coworker in a similar situation volunteers for local search and rescue. It gives him a bigger picture reason to stay in great shape. It’s got me thinking about doing the same as I approach my late 40’s.

I have found a social approach works best for keeping me motivated to work out. My partner is training for a canoe trip in Canada, so we both ride our bikes to the gym twice a week. On both days I go to a weight training class for older adults. I like the work out, the instructors and my classmates. Oh yeah, and they play Beatles music.

I also get yearly DXA scans. Last year my scans were horrible and that motivated me to start regular strength training. This year I have improved and that motivates me to keep working out.

Not everything is mental unfortunately. I have all kinds of motivation and willingness to push myself, but no matter what I do, my body is just not in the condition that it was 10 – 15 years ago, and the aches and pains that result from pushing myself prevent me from doing anything more than walking at this point in my life. So, this advice is great if you don’t have any medical conditions preventing you from pushing yourself, however, I believe that there are many people out there like myself who are not built like Goggins.

I realise you have said you don’t swallow the whole Goggins creed, Mr. Moustache, but Goggins? In any measure? Really?

I am surprised you haven’t learnt by now that always pushing your limits, redlining your body, is not a formula for health, fitness and well-being; it is the road to injury and burnout.

There are countless examples of exercise fanatics who started off thinking, with Nietzsche, that ‘That which doesn’t kill me makes me stronger’. They end up realising that ‘That which doesn’t kill me can still cripple me’.

Just look at poor old Ronnie Coleman. https://youtu.be/kq0Sm4kAp4Y?si=_ma2zjT_WoWVi4wC

But after many injuries, all self-inflicted and therefore avoidable, I have developed a different philosophy: Progress over perfection; You won’t improve from something you can’t recover from; Little by little, step by step, work on your weaknesses and limitations; No brain, no gain.

Could your procrastination stem from thinking that exercise is a gruelling, penitential task? Why not just resolve to show up everyday and just do something — some mobility work, an easy jog, a few sets of easy pull-ups and hanging leg raises? Some days that will put you in the mood to push harder, go further— fine. Other days you can stop there — also fine. Just keep showing up and making deposits into the Bank (or ETF, or whatever) of Fitness. They will add up, and sometimes compound, just like money. Health and fitness is a long game, just like saving and investment.

There is definitely a time and place to test your mettle — generally in a competition or emergency. But suffering is not how you get fitter. ‘The ability to suffer during a workout is just one skill. Don’t over-focus on it. You also need to train a hundred other skills’.https://youtu.be/0h23IANIg6Q For most workouts, the goal should be to finish feeling better than when you started. Energised, not exhausted. If tired, sore, and injured are the side-effects, is it worth it?

Of course, who am I to say what will motivate you? But I know that when I changed my outlook from struggle-&-suffer to small, manageable steps, every day my hesitation vanished and I became keen to show up.

Exactly, I think we’re saying the same thing here. If you read the article, you’ll notice I have no interest in any of the Goggins-style self flogging. It says right in there “reasonable effort”, and I also mentioned that I don’t even need to run ten miles at a time. I’m well aware that overdoing it in any one physical activity leads to injury!

And an interesting side note: doing a healthy amount of strength (weight) training has the opposite effect – it serves as the ultimate injury preventer. I first took up the practice at age 14, making do with those flimsy plastic hand-me-down barbell plates in my tiny bedroom at home. And since then I’ve never had a real physical injury, my knees and back have been miraculously perfect despite all sorts of skiing, snowboarding, mountain biking, moving around wheelbarrows of concrete and carrying washing machines and pianos up and down staircases. My body is a piece of work equipment and I really want it to keep working hard for me for decades to come!

So anyway, I’m only using the Goggins mentality to catch myself when I want to skip out on a difficult thing – whether it’s showing up for what might be an easy workout, or making the phone call to the repair company to get my windshield fixed. Small manageable steps, but I have to DO them.

What is my identity? What is your identity? I’ve always been someone who works out relatively frequently, so that’s who I am. There is no need to extra motivation, I just go. I want to run, it’s fun, I want to lift, it’s fun and makes me look better. It’s like from Dodgeball: Global Gym vs Average Joe’s. You want to improve yourself a little bit, great, but not everyone needs to be super elite perfectionist Global Gym. Taking all of Huberman’s advice is ridiculous. Just be healthy and do you, improve things a little bit. Or find your own goals and do them.
