Insights on building wealth, making informed career decisions, and achieving financial independence from a fellow physician.

Physician on FIRE and The Prudent Plastic Surgeon share a mission to help physicians build financial knowledge, independence, and control over their future.

Dr. Jordan Frey is a full-time practicing plastic surgeon and founder of The Prudent Plastic Surgeon, read by 20,000+ physicians. For five years, he has shared insights on personal finance, investing, career decisions, and financial independence while continuing to practice medicine.

A Physician on FIRE Partnership As part of our partnership, Physician on FIRE periodically shares select articles from The Prudent Plastic Surgeon with its readers.

About three months ago, I decided to actually give physician expert witness work a shot.

It was something that had been on my radar for a while. I knew other physicians did it. I knew it could be a lucrative side gig. And, at least on paper, it seemed to check a lot of the boxes that I look for in a physician side gig.

And three months later, after a bunch of cold outreach, a lot of conversations, a course on expert witness work, and several actual cases, including one involving a zebra, I figured it was a good time to share what I’ve learned so far.

The first thing I learned is that getting started in expert witness work is not particularly exciting.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

There was no moment where I signed up somewhere and cases suddenly started pouring in. Instead, there were a lot of emails, Zoom calls, and phone calls.

I reached out to lawyers. I talked to physicians who were already doing expert witness work. Plus I joined physician expert witness networks. I introduced myself, explained my expertise as a reconstructive plastic surgeon, sent my CV, and basically said, “If you ever need someone like me, keep me in mind.”

And I’ll admit, this felt a little uncomfortable. We aren’t really trained to market ourselves. For me, there was definitely a little bit of a feeling that I was shamelessly promoting myself. But eventually I started thinking about it differently.

We really are experts in our fields. And there are legal cases where an objective medical opinion can legitimately help a patient, a physician, or both. My job isn’t to advocate for whichever attorney happens to hire me. It’s to review the information and give an honest opinion based on my training and experience.

Once I reframed it that way, the outreach became a lot easier.

At the same time, I quickly realized that being an expert physician doesn’t automatically make you an expert witness. I understood the broad strokes. Review the medical records. Understand what happened. Form an opinion. Explain it.

But I didn’t really know how to structure a case review, what attorneys were looking for, how to write a report, how to create a fee schedule, or even how the business side of expert witness work typically operates.

That’s when I took Amy Fogelman’s High Rock Academy expert witness course. I found it incredibly helpful, particularly because it wasn’t just theoretical. There were actual resources and templates that I could use when cases started coming in, including report templates that I ultimately used for my first cases.

That preparation ended up being pretty well timed.

About six weeks after I really started pursuing this, I got my first case.

Ironically, my first case didn’t come from any of the cold outreach I had been doing. It came from a local physician friend who knew an attorney looking for someone with my expertise.

There’s probably an important lesson in there. You can send emails and join directories and market yourself all you want, but relationships still matter. The case involved aesthetic breast surgery and, to this point, has also been my most extensive case. There were a lot of records. There were depositions. And there were hours spent reviewing everything and figuring out exactly what happened.

Then I got on the phone with the attorneys.

This was probably the first time the work really clicked for me. They had very specific questions, and my job was essentially to do something that I already do every day as a physician: take a lot of complicated medical information, figure out what actually matters, form an opinion, and explain that opinion clearly.

That case is actually still ongoing, so there may be more work to come.

But after that first case, others started showing up.

I’ve now reviewed a handful of cases. Some have been relatively run-of-the-mill. And then there was the case involving an injury from a zebra.

I don’t remember that particular scenario coming up during plastic surgery residency.

But even that case reinforced what I’ve come to think is the biggest advantage of expert witness work for physicians: we already know how to do most of this. We spend our careers reviewing information, identifying what is relevant, synthesizing it, forming an assessment, and communicating that assessment to someone else. Sometimes that someone is a patient. Sometimes it’s another physician. And sometimes it’s an insurance company or hospital administrator.

In expert witness work, it happens to be an attorney.

That’s why, after only three months, I think this may be one of the better physician side gigs available. I used to list expert witness work as something I hadn’t personally done yet. Now I can at least start filling in that blank from experience.

Obviously, the income is part of the appeal.

One of the harder things when I started was figuring out what to charge. Talking to physicians who had done this before helped, as did seeing how others structured their fees.

I ultimately landed at $750 per hour with a five-hour minimum retainer.

So when I’m retained, I receive payment upfront for those first five hours. If the work goes beyond that, I bill additional time. I’ve had cases that exceeded the retainer and others that didn’t. But what matters to me isn’t just the hourly rate.

I’ve reviewed records early in the morning before my kids wake up. I’ve done work during their practices. And I’ve worked on cases in between operations while waiting for turnover.

That’s a meaningful distinction from clinical medicine, where income is about as directly tied to our physical presence as you can get. If I’m operating, seeing patients, or taking call, I can make money. If I’m not there, I generally don’t.

Expert witness work is still active income. I’m certainly not going to put it in the same category as the passive income streams I’ve built. But it’s active income on my terms.

Not every potential case turns into actual work.

This is particularly true with expert witness directories and referral companies. You may get contacted about a case, review some preliminary information, give a brief response, and then never hear anything else because the attorney chose someone else.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Do that enough times and it can become a real time suck. That’s one reason why, so far, I’ve preferred building direct relationships with attorneys.

And once you do get a case, my early impression is that the best marketing strategy is probably incredibly simple: Do a good job.

Be responsive. Be timely. You also need to be thorough without writing a 47-page treatise when three pages will do. Answer the questions being asked. Be easy to work with.

And most importantly, be honest. If your opinion isn’t what the attorney wants to hear, that’s still your opinion. The entire value of being an expert witness comes from being objective.

Do those things consistently and, I suspect, repeat business and referrals will follow.

There is one major part of expert witness work that I still haven’t experienced: Testifying.

I haven’t been deposed or testified at trial yet. So that’s an obvious blind spot in everything I’m saying here.

From talking to more experienced physician experts, my understanding is that most cases don’t ultimately involve courtroom testimony. A lot of the work is record review, conversations with attorneys, and written reports. Still, testimony is different. Being questioned by an opposing attorney while defending your opinions is not something we routinely do in clinical medicine.

When I eventually have that experience, I’ll write about it.

Physician expert witness work isn’t passive income. It’s scalable but requires effort, much in the same way that other physician side income streams can potentially require. And it isn’t something where you send a few emails and immediately have an overflowing pipeline of cases.

But it does something that I think is incredibly valuable for physicians.

It takes expertise that we already spent years, really decades, developing and gives us another way to use it. And unexpectedly, I think it has already made me a better physician.

Reading cases retrospectively makes you think differently about documentation. It makes you think about how clinical decisions will look when someone reviews the chart a year later without any of the context you had in the moment. I’ve already found myself bringing some of those lessons back into my own practice.

A handful of hours of expert witness work can generate income comparable to working an extra clinical shift. Except I can do those hours before my kids wake up, at a practice, or whenever else they fit into my life.

And that gets back to the whole reason I’m pursuing financial freedom as a physician in the first place.

The goal isn’t just more money. It’s more control over my time. Three months in, expert witness work seems like a pretty good way to create a little more of both.

#8674. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!)

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.)

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out.  I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:24 am

I read that many of the people in that (wealthy) part of LA were forced to self-insure partly because the insurance companies weren’t willing to cover such a high wildfire risk. At a certain level of wealth, the cost of repairing or rebuilding a house isn’t a big deal but I’m sure there are many people left behind and struggling.

For the rest of us, it’s really just a probability game: if you can’t afford the consequences of a fire or disaster, either buy insurance or stick to a less expensive house. If you ARE getting insurance, do the math on whether the premium is worth the coverage.

Homeowners also includes liability protection if someone is injured on your property and for certain off-property related claims, like if you injure someone with your bicycle, or get sued for slander or libel. Also it generally would be required before one could have an umbrella policy for higher liability coverage. Maybe this is more of a U.S. mindset, than an Canadian one where there are fewer outlandish personal injury judgments, but for me having insurance to protect my net worth is an important consideration. So I carry la homeowner’s policy for asset protection.

This is a very good point. I am a retired insurance regulatory lawyer, and homeowners insurance just covers much more than the house. It covers YOU for liability. If you get sued, it also hires a lawyer to defend you and pays any judgement against you up to the policy limits. It also provides loss of use coverage to pay for the hotel you have to live in if your house becomes uninhabitable AND pays to replace the contents of your house, like your furniture, appliances, and clothes.

You write that, “Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.”

You don’t have home insurance?!?! Say if your house burns down? Isn’t it worth it to have insurance to cover that catastrophic loss? I pay a small amount monthly for this benefit. Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:21 am

Yes, for many people house insurance is a solid plan. And if you have a mortgage on that house, it’s mandatory because the lender wants YOU to pay to protect THEIR collateral.

As you get older and wealthier, and especially if you live in a not-that-expensive house like my current one, it’s worth it to continually rework the math. In my case I came up with these thoughts:

– if my house burned down, I’d be rather pissed but the actual cost of rebuilding would not affect my ability to stay retired – and the foundation would probably survive, which cuts the rebuilding costs by another $50k or so – and I’d rebuild it into a much cooler house – and I’d be the builder and hire all my carpenter friends to work alongside me, because that’s my favorite thing to do anyway!

Another factor is just the “sleep at night” question. If having insurance helps you sleep better at night, that increases the value for you as well. In my case, I sleep like a worry-free log every night anyway :-)

I mean yes, I generally try to be helpful in the ways that I can, both locally and on a bigger scale with things like sharing ideas on the internet. But there’s an (ADHD-informed) balance where I need a certain amount of free time and I work best in an unscheduled life where I only decide what to do most days AFTER a good morning walk and breakfast.

So, some people will start and run their bigger foundations and save more of the world than me. And I’ll keep going on my own smaller scale, mostly in the workshop or the scenic parts of Colorado, having a great time here too.

I so understand this comment and thank you for it.

Wow, so interesting to learn that you have ADHD, too. I just learned that I have ADHD (in my mid 50s), and it has explained a LOT of my life trajectory. And, it has finally explained why I struggle so much with my desk-bound job. Single mom with a teen living in an expensive city (I know…) so no FIRE for me yet, but your posts have kept me on a frugal path for more than a decade, so I thank you. Having a paid-off house with very low costs (solar powered, do a lot of my own repairs) and a rental property I will get there much sooner than I previously thought possible.

This is a great question and conversation starter. I retired early about two years ago, and I’m early in the process of considering these big ideas. I think a lot about how to do the most I can for my community without turning over 100% of my time to somebody else’s goals and whims.

A couple of core principles that I’m drawn to:

1. It’s all about the 80/20 rule — what are the 20% of actions we can take that will make 80% of the change? Pick one thing that aligns with your skills, interests, and influence, and work on that. For MMM, it’s reducing car traffic (and thereby carbon emissions) by persuading people to design their lives around biking. For me, it’s increasing literacy, particularly media literacy. I think if Americans were better able to distinguish propaganda, scams, etc. from good information, we would be much more effective at creating policies that benefit as many people as possible.

2. Giving money can be just as good (or better!!) than giving your time. I completely get MMM’s point here that it’s counterproductive to be locked into running a nonprofit full-time if that’s not how you work best. I believe people who prefer more time freedom can feel great about “just” providing funding for others who find meaning in devoting a lot of time to hands-on work. (And many people, like me, will fall in the middle, with some part-time volunteering and some donating.)

Many of us worry about problems that we have no real expertise in or direct control over, like preventing wildfires. It is a huge contribution to donate money strategically to the people who do have the expertise and the control, even if your time is going only to making art, enjoying nature, hanging out with friends, etc. We learned from MMM that our money works harder than us, and that can apply to charitable giving too!

I’ve been retired for 5 years and moved to a retirement community. I’ve seen how very quickly circumstances can change due to health issues. Last year was a big year…we spent 7 weeks in Europe, did 3 cruises, bought a fancy-pants sports car, built a house for our son so he can start to bank money with no house payment. And with the crazy stock market, our accounts are pretty much the same! I scrimped and micromanaged our household spending for decades…it does feel odd to say “yes” instead of an automatic no. Feel very fortunate to have the choice to spend more on travel, family, charities. I see so many people who are not as fortunate and hope your younger readers are listening to you! My millenial co-workers used to snicker at my frugal ways, sadly. They should start teaching finance in middle school!

> “In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?”

I’m definitely trying to operate more with an abundance mindset these days (thanks to the likes of you, Carl @ 1500 days, and ChooseFI). However, it is difficult to communicate accurately to my wife why I think spending $250 instead of $90 for a flight with more convenient times is fine but spending $15 on McDonald’s is a total waste. To me it is clear: the former results in a better experience and improves the quality of life, the latter reduces my lifespan.

> “A Temporary Note about Teslas and other electric cars: Rumor has it that the $7500 EV tax credit might be disappearing when our new president takes over next week, so this might be the cheapest chance to buy what I feel are the best cars on the market: The Model Y, or Model 3.”

I’ve benefited from the EV tax credit, but at the same time I don’t like the federal government distorting the market, but then also at the same time the federal government already does that in so many areas with ridiculous Byzantine regulations, so the EV tax credit could be seen as a form of “un-distortion”. Either way, if the tax credit disappears I am quite confident that the market will find a new equilibrium all on its own.

I’ve heard that “subsidy/distorted market” argument about EVs so many times over the past few years, and yet I find it mostly irrelevant. I think most people don’t know that the combustion engine vehicles industry has been heavily subsidized for decades, either through tax breaks, direct investments from the government, direct subsidies to oil companies and, in a more subtle way, by very lax environmental regulations that have allowed the production of these vehicles (or oil) at a distorted cost. The only difference is that when buying EVs, consumers receive the tax credit directly instead of getting a hidden discount on a combustion engine vehicle that was subsidized on the production line. So yes, in the end, everything is subsidized in one way or another!

MMM (or others), can you elaborate on the comment, “(plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house)”….exactly what is that? I think I am fairly informed in the world of finance (have been FIREd since 2014 @ age of 40) but not exactly sure what this is. Thank you!

It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). So the subsidy is the reduction in annual spending because of not having the mortgage. But he got that by working at paying off the mortgage earlier in life, which he acknowledges is a trade off.

It sounds like you had a bunch of fun and got to spend “tons” of money without impacting your long term finances, and instead continuing to let them grow.

I’d like to see you up the ante in 2025 and do an MMM experiment where you spend exactly a 4% withdrawal rate on that theoretical million dollar retirement account.

Let me know if you need help spending the extra 10k :)

To keep things non-promotional, please use a real name or nickname(not Blogger @ My Blog Name)

The most useful comments are those written with the goal of learning from or helping out other readers – after reading the whole article and all the earlier comments. Complaints and insults generally won’t make the cut here, but by all means write them on your own blog!

You read that right, we’re bringing the holiday spirit earlier this year with a discussion on how early is early enough to start planning for the holiday frenzy.

Fall starts, and before you’ve finished raking a single leaf, Halloween candy is on clearance and you’re staring down two straight months of travel, shopping, gifts and family logistics.

Most people categorize this as an emotional gauntlet. It’s a time for family and mayhem, making new memories and reliving old ones.

For physicians, or any high earner really,  it’s also a financial trial. Having high income doesn’t magically make holiday spending a breeze. If anything, your wealth-building habits are put to their hardest test in November and December. It’s hard to be a spectator when everyone around you is spending like they’ve never heard of a budget.

Planning now, while the season still feels far off, is one of the ways you can get ahead of the season and its temptations.

The average American planned to spend around $890 per person last year on gifts, food, decorations and other seasonal costs, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual survey. That figure is the second highest in the survey’s 23-year history.

Last year, a Gallup survey found that consumers expected to spend $1,007 on gifts alone but that figure dropped to $778 by the time November actually arrived. That’s usually when the early enthusiasm comes face to face with the actual bank balance.

A family of four routinely spends $3,500 to $4,000 across the full season with travel and entertaining accounted for.

Those are reasonable numbers, some might even call them conservative. Which is fine as long as they align with the budget. But what happens when the spending exceeds what you had planned for?

In 2024, 36% of Americans took on new debt to cover holiday costs, averaging $1,181. Less than half (44%) of them expected to end up there. Average credit card balances aren’t slowing down either. According to Forbes, consumers, on average, owe more than $6,500.

Physicians aren’t immune to this. Heck, they might even be more vulnerable. High earners overspend for the same reason everyone else does. Decisions made in December, under time pressure, during the busiest clinical stretch of the year, have a way of getting out of hand.

Last year, Deloitte’s Holiday Retail Survey found that 57% of consumers expected the economy to weaken over the following six months, the most negative outlook Deloitte had recorded since it started tracking sentiment back in 1997.

Travel analyst Katy Nastro told Vox that domestic flights are typically best booked 3 to 7 months out, and international flights 4 to 10 months out. Booking your December trips in late September can be a gamechanger.

Rental cars follow the same logic. You don’t need to pay upfront, so reserving one now costs nothing and protects you from the price climb once inventory shrinks closer to the holidays.

Forbright Bank’s internal data on recurring deposits found that customers who automate savings consistently saw about 5 times the growth of those who don’t.

A 2025 survey found that 38% of Americans had already started holiday shopping by the first week of September last year. 66% said that they planned to shop earlier than usual.

For a physician working full clinical hours, that invisible labor is a direct hit to the recovery time you need between shifts.

There’s also a well-documented cognitive cost to decision-making under pressure. Research on decision fatigue has repeatedly found that the quality of a person’s choices declines the more decisions they’ve already made that day.

Spreading holiday decisions across three months instead of cramming them into three weeks in December means less mental fatigue for the person who has to manage it all.

This is the most understandable objection, and also the one early planning actually solves.

I’m not suggesting you build a full itinerary this weekend. Take one task at a time like booking a flight or automating that recurring transfer. It can also be something as simple as asking family members what gifts they want this year.

Waiting for a specific sale date isn’t the savings strategy many of us think it is.

Investing can feel exhausting when your work is already packed with tasks. Amid meetings, deadlines, family responsibilities, and day-to-day duties, it is unrealistic to allocate several hours of your day to market research.

The good part is that you don’t need to keep investing in research all the time to be a successful investor. All it takes is a small routine that keeps your knowledge current and gives you a sense of market developments without enslaving you to research.

The very beginning of it all is to set up a system that allows you to monitor major market events efficiently without drowning in too many online financial sites each morning.

Professionals use AlphaWire and similar platforms to access the latest news and details on individual companies quickly.

Learn what Class A, B, and C really mean, how building quality affects distributions and resale, and why some passive investors prefer properties outside the top tier.

Using one main source of financial updates makes it much easier to see what is happening, and it significantly reduces the time you waste digging through different platforms.

This organized method of gathering stock market information can help you build and maintain your research routine over time.

One of the first things you can do is, for example, identify the companies that have been gaining traction, significant corporate news, movements in the stock markets, etc. You can then decide which of these topics merit further in-depth analysis.

It’s not about knowing everything or reading all the content out there. Set up a system that brings only the essential stuff to your attention so you can use your time effectively.

For many busy people, the 10 minutes or so they spend at the end of the workday isn’t enough to stay familiar with market developments.

Following the entire stock market at once is an easy way to waste time. In fact, one might think that a watchlist would be too limiting, but in reality, the opposite is true.

Your watchlist can include companies that you already own as well as companies that you are considering buying, a couple of their major rivals, and some key market indices related to the style you are using in your investment portfolio.

The watchlist would normally look like this:

The research boundaries have been limited in this way. When you ask yourself questions like, ‘What did the market do today?’ you will find answers that matter to the portfolio you follow by switching your question around.

https://unsplash.com/photos/stock-market-chart-displayed-on-laptop-screen-IrRbSND5EUc

It is a mistake to think you should complete all your daily research at once. You can divide the tasks across the week.

For example, Monday and Wednesday could be update days, while the other days could be for watchlist reviews and company reading sessions.

Differentiating the routine this way will help you stick with it. Dedicate a 30-minute session or a full-day activity during the weekend for conducting thorough research whenever needed.

Eventually, those short, regular sessions will give you such a solid grounding in your research that you will find it much easier to interpret and analyze any development.

Writing a journal of what you discover in the process of investing research is a good idea because it will be a great tool for your further study.

Your journals serve you as your personal library where you keep track of all your findings and research.

Later on, for instance, when you want to start anew on a topic, there should be no need for you to go back and read everything. You can remind yourself what you were thinking about and what you have learned before, and match it with what is going on now.

In general, it is good to know the difference so you don’t think a piece of news always leads to a buying or selling decision.

The idea behind investment research is to learn about and become familiar with the company or investment idea.

It may be a good practice to read about one stock repeatedly over time, but unless its changes are significant enough, you won’t make up your mind. That’s how it should be, because the more information you collect, the better your base understanding of the business, industry, and the company’s performance.

When you finally get a major piece of information about the company, you will immediately know the background without having to refer back to all your previous notes.

#8667. Air France-KLM Flying Blue → Tahiti Business Class

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:

The Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most important rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

This is a moderate-difficulty booking. The steps themselves aren't complicated — but the sequencing matters enormously. Follow this in order.

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. You do NOT need a Flying Blue account to search — but you will need one to book, so create a free account if you haven't already. Search LAX → PPT in business class. Flying Blue's calendar view lets you scan across multiple departure dates, which is essential for spotting availability on a route with limited award seats.

Tip: Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. For a route this popular and this capacity-constrained, searching at the 11-month mark is strongly advised. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 359 days before your target travel dates.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its new Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. Bookmark flyingblue.com/en/earn-spend/flying-blue-promo-rewards and check it monthly. If Tahiti appears, act immediately — Promo Reward availability disappears fast.

Once you find available dates and seats, note the exact miles price shown at checkout. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the cost you see on Monday might differ from Thursday. Screenshot the search result with the price clearly visible. This is your confirmation that the award is priceable before you transfer points.

Now — and only now — transfer your points:

Transfer the exact amount you need — no more, no less.

Return to flyingblue.com, complete the search again with your now-funded account, and book. Have your passport and traveler details ready. Pay any taxes/fees (usually $50–$150 on non-Promo awards; near-zero on Promo Rewards) with a travel rewards credit card to earn additional points.

Award availability on this route moves quickly. If your target dates are sold out:

Flying Blue uses dynamic award pricing, which usually makes award charts unpredictable. But the monthly Promo Rewards program creates a fixed-price overlay that dramatically undercuts the dynamic rates. When Tahiti appears on the Promo Rewards list, business class pricing drops 25 to 50 percent below standard and fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. Air France is the sole operator of the LAX to PPT nonstop — no other airline flies it — which means Flying Blue is the only loyalty program with direct booking access to this route. This combination of route exclusivity and periodic promotional pricing is what makes this a genuine sweet spot rather than just a good redemption.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a couple planning their 10th anniversary trip to Bora Bora in the spring of 2026. They want to start the trip right — meaning lie-flat seats over the Pacific, not a middle seat in economy for a nine-hour flight.

The cash price: Air France business class from LAX to PPT in spring typically runs $6,500–$9,000 per person round-trip. For two people, you're looking at $13,000–$18,000. That's a car payment for most families. Even if it's in the travel budget, it's a brutal number to justify when you're pursuing financial independence.

The points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. For two passengers: 176,000 Flying Blue miles total, plus approximately $200–$300 in taxes and carrier fees (less if you catch a Promo Rewards release, where surcharges are waived entirely).

The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

What you'll actually experience: You check in at LAX and are directed to the business class line — a detail that still feels quietly luxurious no matter how many times you've done it. Once onboard the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet in length. The cabin's reduced cabin pressure and higher humidity mean you arrive in Papeete meaningfully less fatigued than you would in economy — important when you have a connecting boat ride to Bora Bora ahead of you.

Air France's catering reflects its French heritage: expect a proper multi-course meal service, a curated wine selection, and warm bread — not a foil-wrapped tray. The flight is roughly 8–9 hours nonstop, so there's time to genuinely sleep, watch a film, and arrive rested.

For a couple using points they accumulated from normal household spending over 12–18 months, the $16,000 in combined cash value they didn't spend is the real number — and the one that matters most on the path to FI.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on the first of every month. Set a phone reminder. These promotions offer 25–50% off standard award pricing AND eliminate fuel surcharges. On a Promo Rewards release, an 88,000-mile business class award could drop to as low as 44,000–66,000 miles with no surcharges. That's the difference between good and extraordinary. Don't miss a cycle.

Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. The LAX–PPT route operates a single daily nonstop on a single aircraft — meaning business class inventory is finite and competitive. If you're targeting holidays, school break windows, or peak Tahiti season (July–August), mark your calendar to search at the 11-month mark.

Flying Blue permits open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into PPT and return from a different city — or fly from a different origin. This flexibility can reduce deadhead positioning flights and help families traveling from cities other than Los Angeles build more logical itineraries.

This is the cardinal sin of award booking. Transferred points cannot be reversed. Never move miles to Flying Blue until you have confirmed award availability on your exact dates with a price you've screenshotted. Chase, Amex, and Citi all transfer instantly — use that speed advantage after you've confirmed the seat exists.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the same route can cost meaningfully different amounts day-to-day and even hour-to-hour. Don't assume the price from your earlier search is locked in. Always verify at checkout before transferring.

Because Flying Blue accepts transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, and Bilt at 1:1, your earning strategy is flexible. Focus on a single flexible currency — the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve for Ultimate Rewards, or the Amex Gold/Platinum for Membership Rewards — and let everyday spending build toward the 88,000-mile target over 12–18 months.

Marriott transfers to Flying Blue at 3:1 — meaning 264,000 Marriott points become 88,000 Flying Blue miles. Unless you have a massive Marriott balance you can't use elsewhere, this is an inefficient path. Stick to the 1:1 partners.

This redemption is purpose-built for couples and families planning a landmark trip to French Polynesia — an anniversary, a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or simply the trip you've been telling yourself you'd take "someday." If Tahiti or Bora Bora is on the life list, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.

Minimum requirements: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person for round-trip business class, plus approximately $100–$300 in taxes (less on Promo Rewards). For a couple, plan for 176,000 transferable points minimum.

For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents the travel rewards philosophy at its best: redirecting the value of everyday spending into genuinely transformative experiences, without derailing the path to financial independence.

Register for free at flyingblue.com. Enable email notifications for Promo Rewards announcements. Set a calendar reminder for the 1st of each month to check the new promo routes the moment they are released.

Use the Flying Blue award search calendar view to scan business class availability on the LAX to PPT route across multiple dates. Check both standard pricing and Promo Rewards pricing. Do not transfer any points until you confirm available seats.

Once you confirm award space, transfer the required miles from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Only transfer after confirming availability.

Complete the booking on flyingblue.com as soon as your miles arrive. Select your preferred lie-flat seat through the seat map. For couples, choose adjacent seats in the business cabin. Promo Rewards availability is limited and can disappear within hours.

Standard dynamic pricing typically runs around 88,000 miles one-way in business class from LAX to Papeete. When Tahiti appears on the monthly Promo Rewards list, that price can drop to 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges — a savings of 25 to 50 percent.

Tahiti is not guaranteed every month. Flying Blue rotates destinations across its network. You may see Tahiti appear several times per year, especially during shoulder season. The key is having your points ready and checking on the 1st of every month so you can act immediately when it appears.

The nonstop Air France flight to Tahiti only departs from LAX. However, you can book a connecting itinerary through flyingblue.com that includes a domestic connection to LAX on the same award ticket. Alternatively, book a separate positioning flight to LAX using a different program.

No. One of the defining benefits of Promo Rewards is that fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. You pay only the mile cost plus minimal taxes and airport fees, typically $60 to $100 per direction. This is a significant advantage over standard Flying Blue pricing, which can include carrier-imposed surcharges.

Flying Blue to Tahiti in business class is a genuinely unique sweet spot because no other loyalty program can book this route. The only nonstop from the US to French Polynesia operates exclusively on Air France out of LAX, and Flying Blue is the only way to book it with miles. At Promo Rewards pricing of 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way, you are getting a $6,500 or more experience for transferable points that most ChooseFI members already hold. Set your monthly reminder, keep 80,000 to 100,000 points in reserve, and book the moment Tahiti appears on the promo list. For couples planning a milestone trip to Bora Bora or Moorea, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.

We spend an enormous amount of time looking at rich people. Entire industries exist to tell us what billionaires are buying, what CEOs make, what a software engineer earns, and how much some influencer paid for her house. Yet a huge share of American wealth sits inside businesses and assets that produce almost no cultural footprint at all.

The financial media love to spin a story about AI taking over the planet and humans becoming redundant but you know what the fear mongers are missing? The fact that all our prosperity does not come from the financial system or the stock market. Prosperity comes from productivity.

How we feel about AI risk is instructive of where investors often go wrong when dealing with risk. We deal with risk in a very human fashion. We learn from emotive experiences and focus on what is happening right in front of our eyes. We judge risks based on how they make us feel.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

The reality is that 25-34-year-olds are increasingly living with their parents. In 2025, 49% of adults under 30 lived with a parent, up 12 percentage points from 2019, according to the Federal Reserve’s Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households survey published earlier this year. The reasons aren’t necessarily surprising.

Talking about money is very hard, especially if you learned from an early age that doing it was inappropriate, awkward, or not even your place in a relationship. But finding the courage to communicate is only the first hurdle. How we communicate can be an equal challenge.

Most wealthy retirees either overconfidently blow through their assets (rare) or cautiously refuse to touch the principal (typical). Did you know that most retirees manage to live and die happily without ever even hearing the words “Roth conversion” or “IRMAA?” Many of them can’t even tell you their tax bracket!

You may have spent years planning to retire at a specific age, only to discover that the timing is not entirely yours to control. The job you assumed would carry you to your planned retirement date may no longer be there, and the financial plan built around that timeline may need to change with it. That is why retirement planning should not depend too heavily on a single age, a specific account balance, or a rigid view of the future.

For couples with a big age gap, the number of moving parts multiplies. Financial planners characterize the process as essentially having to knit together two different retirement trajectories and make it work for one family.

Sometimes we go completely down the personal finance rabbit hole. We use frugality as a weapon. We track every single cent we spend. We obsess over our investments, constantly maximizing the tax code, and agonizing over the minor differences between traditional and Roth accounts. We become so hyper-focused on the efficiency of our financial machine that we forget why we built it in the first place.

The tax benefits of a Health Savings Account (HSA) effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary. That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account in an effort to maximize the tax benefits.

Somewhere on page two of nearly every syndication deck sits a letter grade, and most of us read “Class A” the way we read an A on a board exam: good, safe, move on. That habit costs physicians money.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

The letter describes a building. Your returns depend on what the sponsor paid for it, what it costs to keep standing, and who will want it when the hold period ends. Picture a 1985 garden-style complex with original roofs and tired HVAC units. Those replacements show up as capital expenditures, and every dollar spent on a new chiller is a dollar that never reaches your distribution check. Flip it around and a gleaming new tower can still disappoint if the sponsor overpaid at purchase, since a deep bench of institutional buyers at exit can’t rescue a bad entry price.

On Tuesday, October 6, Tyler Farrelly and Jacob Maggy of Realberry join Physician on FIRE to take the label apart. You’ll leave knowing how to weigh a property’s class against the projections stacked on top of it, and how a building’s age trickles down to a limited partner’s cash flow. They’ll walk through 2026 data showing office, multifamily and hospitality performance splitting by quality. Resale gets real attention too, which matters when you can’t exactly unload an LP stake on a slow Tuesday afternoon. Expect an honest case for why some seasoned investors deliberately buy below the top tier.

Save your free seat for October 6 at 6 PM ET (3 PM PT).

#8662. Debt And Physician Finances

Have you ever had a termite infestation? You likely didn’t realize you did until it was too late. For months or sometimes years, you go about your life without the faintest idea that something is afoot, because after all, the house looks just fine from the driveway.

By the time you notice that sagging floorboards, the structure is already compromised.

Debt is that termite infestation. You don’t realize the damage it’s doing until it’s too late. It gnaws through your income, unnoticed, until the day a job change, a market downturn or an unplanned expense reveals just how rickety the foundation has become.

More than a third of Americans earning $200,000 or more say they’re living paycheck to paycheck. Nearly a third of six-figure earners describe themselves as financially stretched, struggling, or drowning.

Physicians are not exempt from this. A high income means nothing on its own. It can open up opportunities, yes but those options feel out of reach when debt takes away the majority of your paycheck.

Student loans and a primary mortgage are fixtures of adulthood. If you’re a physician and have never had to carry these, you’re extremely lucky. Or you know something I don’t— in which case, please share your secret with the rest of us.

The median education debt for the class of 2025 was $215,000— not including undergraduate loans. Many physicians carry this into their 40s and 50s.

Nobody becomes a doctor debt-free unless family money covers the tab. In return you get to enjoy a career in medicine earning good money with plenty of lucrative options for supplementing that income.

The mortgage on a primary residence is an equally unavoidable aspect of adult finances. In return you get a place to call home and an asset that (usually) appreciates. Mortgage is debt, yes, but paying it down builds equity that would otherwise go to someone else in the form of rent.

This type of debt cannot be categorized as termites. This is the foundation you build on top of and most physicians manage it fine once attending income kicks in. There are also ways to significantly ease the burden on this type of debt.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Credit card balances, car payments beyond what a reliable car would cost, a second home bought at the top of a market, an extravagant vacation you didn’t save for but financed instead— I could go on. These are all examples of bad debt. Not because they aren’t “profitable” but also because the ROI they provide is short-lived.

Having a lake house feels great but not if you have to put up with a toxic workplace in order to pay it off. Jetting off to Switzerland feels like freedom but not if you have to skimp on your 401(k) contributions for the following years in order to pay it off.

In the second quarter of 2026, the average APR on credit card accounts that carry a balance was 22.15%, up from 21.52% in Q1. Total U.S. credit card debt reached $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, closing in on the all-time high of $1.28 trillion set at the end of 2025. Roughly 60% of cardholders carry a balance month to month rather than paying in full.

A $15,000 balance at 22% APR costs over $3,300 a year in interest alone, money that produces nothing, builds nothing and simply vanishes. Extended across a decade of minimum payments, the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase several times over.

A 43-year-old high-earner drowning in debt posted his story on Reddit. Let’s call him Bill.

“On the outside, I probably look like a success. On the inside, I feel like I’m slowly breaking — just getting through one day at a time,” he wrote.

Him and his spouse carry close to $1 million in combined loans. Both work high-paying jobs. On paper, they look fine. In practice, their special-needs son’s therapy costs $3,000 a month. Before his diagnosis, that $3000 was the extra income they had planned to put towards paying down debt. These are the kind of curveballs life can throw at you. Out of nowhere, unannounced— thwack.

Bill tried his hand at several side businesses which failed and added more debt on top. He describes feeling trapped in a career he doesn’t enjoy with no visible exit.

Close to $1 million is debt may sound insane but in New York, D.C. or California, that number is an easy target. HCOL is no joke and Bill’s situation isn’t unique. Debt can be enticing even to the best of us.

Bill’s failure stems from the fact that he had thought nothing would ever go wrong and he would be able to pay off

the debt from the extra income. It was that years of “should be fine” income had never been forced into a written plan, so a single disruption ate the entire buffer.

That’s the sinkhole version of debt. It doesn’t look like reckless spending from the outside. It looks like a normal life that happens to be standing on ground with nothing underneath it.

Also read: Is Driving a Honda Smarter Than Flexing a Ferrari?

We love compound interest but not when it’s on the other side. Compound interest grows our savings the same way it grows balances— with indifferent efficiency.

Every month a balance carries over at 20%+ APR, that growth compounds against the borrower. Over 20 years, that comes out to 52.83x of the original number which could easily mean the difference between a paid-off house and a large credit card bill that never seems to shrink.

Every debt payment carries two costs. The first is obvious: the dollars leaving the account each month. The second almost never gets counted, because it never shows up anywhere: opportunity cost.

The cost of what you give up when your dollars go towards debt when they could’ve gone towards something profitable.

Consider a physician making aggressive payments on $215,000 in student loans during the first years as an attending.

Once the balance hits zero, that monthly cash flow can now go towards investment instead of paying a loan servicer. It can now be invested in index funds, a retirement account or a rental property that produces income instead of consuming it.

Also read: Building Wealth: Lessons In Sustainable Investment for Physicians

That’s what makes debt a double hit. Stretched across a 30-year investing timeline, missed growth frequently outweighs the interest itself, sometimes by a wide margin.

That’s why many advisors suggest building a straightforward financial foundation before reaching for anything advanced. Boring, broadly diversified investing beats clever debt-servicing strategies almost every time because it lets compounding start earlier instead of later.

The next time you sit down to fine-time your financial plan, consider the following:

Learn more: Is Diversification Finally Working Again?

After a decade of deferred spending, attending income brings much-need relief. But with it, comes the temptation to catch up all at once.

Those one-third of six-figure households that feel “stretched, struggling, or drowning” I mentioned earlier?

Their biggest downfall is precisely the fact that every income jump they are blessed with gets absorbed by a bigger house, a nicer car and a few thousand extra dollars a year in subscriptions and shopping. The brokerage accounts become the stepchildren that never get any love or attention.

Don’t be the evil stepmother. Do this instead:

Everyone takes stress as a given. As children we’re conditioned to worry about our homework and grades, as we grow older, we worry about fitting in, dating and winning the rat race.

The joys of parenthood are symbiotic with the worries of how to raise and protect our children in a world like ours. Being alive is, in essence, being stressed.

Debt adds in another layer of stress to all of that. But this is one we usually push away to the back of our minds so much so that it stops registering as stress at all.

Anyone carrying a meaningful balance knows what I’m talking about. Unexpected car repairs make us flinch. Due dates feel heavy but they arrive and we pay; then do it again the following month. Progress feels theoretical.

A systematic review of 39 U.S. studies found that debt is consistently linked to higher rates of stress and even suicide. The authors pointed to financial strain and the pressure of collection as the major drivers. Some debt, such as a mortgage, was labeled as “secure” which proves the point that not all debt is bad.

Another study reports that over-indebted consumers have lower life satisfaction and poorer health due to a diminished sense of control.

Eventually the discomfort becomes the baseline, and that’s when people take on more debt, because an actual plan to eliminate it no longer feels realistic.

Financing makes this worse by design. Nearly every major purchase now arrives with a monthly payment option built in, because a payment feels smaller than a price tag even when the total cost is higher.

47% of Buy Now, Pay Later users have been late on at least one loan in the past year. That percentage had been rising steadily, as it was 41% in 2025 and just 34% in 2024.

More alarmingly, 54% of consumers say that they wouldn’t be able to make ends meet without these loans. 29% say they use them to pay for groceries.

Financial well-being research consistently finds that experiences with debt and credit correlate directly with how secure people feel about their finances, independent of income.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

So the relief once you’re on the other side? It’s exhilarating.

A Gallup study found that among recent graduates, only 25% of those with more than $50,000 in debt were thriving financially compared to 40% of debt-free grads.

Physicians who’ve finished paying off credit cards or student loans, especially after years of aggressive payments alongside PSLF, will know what I’m talking about. The financial change is expected but the psychological weight lifting is what often catches you off guard.

If you want to experience that relief sooner rather than later, stick to aggressive repayment and steer clear of financing anything marketed by its monthly payment instead of its total cost.

Debt is sneaky like that. It can make you feel like you’re living your best life, doing better than ever— doing better than those around you. It’s a costly little dog and pony show.

Home equity products are the easiest way to explain this. A physician spends years building equity in a primary residence, then starts seeing offers to unlock that equity through a HELOC (home equity line of credit) or cash-out refinance for a kitchen remodel, debt consolidation, etc.

The homeowner is essentially being gaslit into converting equity that already belongs to them into a new long-term loan that accrues interest all over again.

These ventures can make sense in rare, high-planned situations tied to high-returns but not in cases where the motive is discretionary. Saving for a large purchase takes longer than financing it yes, but it also provides security which a new, bigger loan just cannot.

No matter how fancy it looks. Debt servicers know how to market their products well. They disguise shackles as flexibility, but really they’re coming for the wealth you’ve already built while claiming to make more for you.

Your home equity is your net worth, not spendable cash. Unless “unlocking it” funds something that generates income or measurable value.

A fee-only advisor is your best friend when it comes to dealing with offers for HELOC or cash-out refinancing. Before you decide anything, compare the total interest cost to how much you could save in 12–24 months for the same purchase before signing anything. The number might surprise you.

Debt is not a moral failing. Nobody builds a career in medicine— or anything for that matter,  without borrowing something along the way. But building wealth that lasts (preferably for generations) requires you to differentiate between good and bad debt.

Student loans, a reasonable mortgage and car payments aside, if you find yourself dreading the monthly payments you know will eat chunks out of your salary, maybe a new plan is what you’re missing.

If any of this hits close to home, you don’t have to figure it out alone. The PoF community is here to help. Drop a comment or take a look at the resources on our site made specifically for this.

And if you’ve already beaten your debt, I want to hear from you. What actually worked? What almost derailed you? Share your story in the comments. Someone reading this today is looking for proof it’s possible— you’re it.

The median for the class of 2025 was $215,000. That number doesn’t include undergraduate loans, so many physicians carry more once you add those in.

Yes. Almost nobody finishes medical school and residency debt free unless family money paid for it. The debt itself isn’t the red flag. What you do with your income once you start earning is.

Match your employer’s 401(k) contribution first, then pay off anything charging more than 6-7% interest. After that, split extra cash between debt and investing based on your rate.

Debt tied to something that produces income or builds equity. A mortgage or a loan on a rental property qualifies. A financed vacation or a car loan on something you can’t actually afford does not.

Yes, for those who qualify. Ten years of qualifying payments while working for a nonprofit or government employer wipes out the remaining balance. Confirm your employer and loan type qualify before counting on it.

As fast as possible. Average APR on carried balances sat at 22.15% in Q2 2026. At that rate, minimum payments can take over a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchase.

Absolutely. Over a third of people earning $200,000 or more report living paycheck to paycheck. Income buys options. Debt takes them away just as fast.

Rarely, unless the money goes toward something that generates income or real value. Most of the time it just converts equity you already own into a new loan with new interest.
