IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

#8640. What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

Some products in this article are from our partners. Read our Advertiser Discloser.

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

Most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

For most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:

After three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

This is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

One of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

You do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

If you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single company’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small

Things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market

Research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That said, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

The key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

#8639. JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

Not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

#8638. Trick or Treatment: The Spookiest Things Physicians Learn About Being Human

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Nothing in residency prepared me for the cadaver head course. Severed heads rested face up in disposable roasting pans, lined down a row of tables, while surgeons calmly rehearsed facelifts. I kept my coffee down, though it was close.

Consider the advantages. These patients won’t ask about downtime or bring up a cousin’s botched eyelid job, and the state board will hear nothing from them. Somebody should study their satisfaction scores.

Medicine has always practiced on the dead, and for a long stretch it practiced on dead people who never agreed to the arrangement.

Nineteenth-century anatomy schools bought corpses from grave robbers and asked few questions about provenance. In Edinburgh in 1828, William Burke and William Hare decided digging was too slow, murdered sixteen people, and sold the bodies to anatomist Robert Knox.

Britain answered with the Anatomy Act of 1832, which handed medical schools the unclaimed bodies of the poor. Reform, of a sort.

Physicians have spent centuries trying to pin down the second a person stops being a person. We have never once nailed it.

In 1905, a French doctor named Beaurieux stood beside the guillotine as a convict named Languille lost his head. Beaurieux called out the man’s name. By his own report, the eyelids lifted and the eyes fixed on him before closing, and the trick worked a second time before it quit for good.

Consciousness or reflex? Nobody could say then, and we can’t now.

Cleveland, 1970. Neurosurgeon Robert White transplanted the head of one rhesus monkey onto the body of another, and the head woke up and tracked people around the room. White spent the rest of his career insisting the operation could work in humans.

I met my own version of this riddle at the bedside of a brain-dead organ donor. He was warm and pink. His heart pumped, his kidneys made urine, and at one point a spinal reflex lifted his arm off the sheet, the move clinicians call the Lazarus sign.

The nurse beside me didn’t flinch. I did. Legally he had died hours earlier, and the procurement team was already en route.

Hospice taught me the rest. Dying unfolds over hours or days, a slow dimming no monitor captures cleanly, yet the death certificate demands a single timestamp. So we pick one and move on.

For several centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up mummy as medicine. Physicians prescribed it for bruises, bleeding and a long menu of complaints, and when genuine Egyptian stock ran short, enterprising suppliers manufactured fresh “mummy” from whatever bodies they could find.

Folklore adds “mellified man,” a corpse supposedly steeped in honey for a century and sold by the chunk. Historians doubt he ever existed. I’ve seen supplement labels make bolder claims.

The dead, for all their weirdness, behave predictably. They stay where you put them. The living refuse that courtesy.

Beginning in the early 2000s, hundreds of children in Sweden withdrew into a state that looked like coma. Nearly all came from asylum-seeking families facing deportation.

They quit eating and talking, then quit opening their eyes, and some stayed that way for a year or longer while parents turned them in bed and nurses ran their feeding tubes. Swedish doctors named it uppgivenhetssyndrom. Resignation syndrome.

Scans came back clean, and so did the labs. Nobody found a virus, a toxin or a lesion. The condition clustered almost entirely inside Swedish borders, and many of the children surfaced slowly once their families won permission to stay.

That makes a lot of physicians squirm. The suffering is real, the paralysis is real, and the driver is a mind expressing despair in the shape its surroundings taught it to take.

I’ve watched a milder version play out in hospice more times than I can count. A patient holds steady for weeks, the family meeting goes sideways, and by the next morning he has stopped eating.

In the Kazakh village of Kalachi, starting around 2013, residents began dozing off mid-sentence. Some slept for days and woke with no memory of it. A shuttered Soviet uranium mine sat down the road, which made for a tidy villain.

Officials tested the air, water and soil, and the government eventually relocated much of the town. Plenty of clinicians point instead to a community watching its jobs and young people drain away, taking any sense of a future with them.

Le Roy, New York, ran a similar script in 2011. A cluster of high school girls developed tics, jerks and verbal outbursts that spread through the school and lit up the evening news.

Erin Brockovich showed up to investigate a chemical spill from a 1970 train derailment. Neurologists diagnosed conversion disorder, a label the families received with roughly the enthusiasm you’d expect.

I’ve delivered that diagnosis myself. The MRI was perfect, the legs still wouldn’t move, and the patient heard “it’s all in your head” no matter how carefully I phrased it. She left to find a doctor who would order another scan.

A toxin is a gift, because it blames no one. A functional diagnosis blames no one either, yet patients hear an accusation in it, and plenty of us deliver it like one. We fumble that conversation more often than we fumble a central line.

Among the Miskito people on Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast, young women fall prey to grisi siknis. They collapse, then bolt into the night, and later describe a dark stranger who came to carry them off.

Capital protection and double-digit monthly cash flow, without becoming a landlord.

Tue, Oct 13  ·  10:00 am PT  ·  11:00 am MT  ·  1:00 pm ET

Village healers treat it with rituals and herbs, and it hops from one community to the next like a bad cold.

Wealthy countries have their own spirits. In El Carmen de Bolívar, Colombia, in 2014, schoolgirls began fainting and convulsing after HPV vaccination. Videos of their episodes ricocheted across social media, and the country’s HPV vaccination rate collapsed.

Two years later, American diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds, and the press settled on a mysterious energy weapon. Some neurologists argue for a more mundane explanation that nobody in Washington wanted to hear.

Our culture supplies the toxins, the radio waves and the MRI that might at last catch the culprit. The Miskito get a dark stranger, while our demons come with CPT codes.

Funerals are where the haunted house collides with your financial plan. The National Funeral Directors Association put the 2023 median cost of a funeral with viewing and burial at about $8,300, and a funeral with cremation at roughly $6,280. Your aunt’s flower budget comes extra.

Whole-body donation to a medical school typically covers transport and cremation and returns the ashes to family, often at little or no cost. Programs vary, so call the school before you count on it.

Your body could spend its retirement crash-testing airbags or showing some nervous first-year where the brachial plexus hides. Mine would be in good company. I still owe that woman with the coral nail polish.

Physicians spend years making sure the 401(k) has a beneficiary. Few of us spend ten minutes deciding who gets the rest of the estate, meaning the part with the liver in it. Put it in writing this Halloween, somewhere between the will and the trust, and let your remains keep earning after you clock out.

Sixty-Nine Percent of the S&P 500 Fell 15% in a Year the Index Gained 26%

That number came up about twenty minutes into Tuesday’s session with Carson Henderson from Earned, and it changed how I think about my own brokerage account. I’d always assumed harvesting was something you did in a crash. Turns out the losses are there every year, buried inside individual lots, waiting for someone to notice.

Carson walked through the whole thing for an hour and the replay is now up. The wash-sale rule and how it reaches into your spouse’s IRA and your dividend reinvestment settings. Why short-term versus long-term matters more than most of us realize. A case study of a 45-year-old radiologist in Utah who sold his imaging centers for $10.5 million and is projected to save $1.1 million in tax through losses harvested ahead of the installment payments. And a tidbit at the end about crypto that I hadn’t heard anywhere else.

The attendee questions were sharper than mine, which I’ll take as a sign the audience is paying attention.

Two months remain before December 31. The replay runs an hour and the moves it covers take an afternoon.

Do you think a million-dollar term life insurance policy sounds like too much insurance?

As a Certified Financial Planner, I see underinsured people every day.

A million-dollar term life insurance policy might actually be the minimum coverage needed for the typical middle-class household, but it’s affordable.

That might sound like an exaggeration, but if you crunch the numbers – just as we’ll be doing a little bit – you’ll realize that a million-dollar policy might be just what you need.

The good news is term life insurance isn’t nearly as costly as most people think.

What makes term life insurance even better is that larger policies cost less on a per thousand basis than smaller policies do. You may find the premium on a $1 million policy is only a little bit higher than it is for $500,000.

Probably, but let’s find out. A general rule of thumb is that you should get 10x your income as baseline coverage for life insurance.

If you’re young, that may be low because you may want to provide your family with enough to replace your income for 15 years or more.

Today, $1 million has become the new baseline for life insurance by a primary breadwinner. Anything less could leave your family financially impaired.

Here’s a list of all the different obligations you may want to have life insurance cover in the unfortunate event you pass away early.

Now that you have an idea of these obligations, let’s punch them into this life insurance calculator to find out if you need a million-dollar policy.

According to Policy Genius, the average cost for a 20-year $1 million term life insurance policy for a 35-year-old male is $53 per month. However, your rate will vary according to the following factors.

The best, and easiest place to start is online. I recommend having two or three insurers compete for your business to make sure you get the best rate and coverage. To see how cheap term life can be, choose your state from the map above to be matched with top life insurance providers instantly.

Let’s look at the individual components that can quickly add up to over a million-dollar policy.

This is where things can get a bit intimidating. Even if you earn a modest income, you may need close to $1 million to replace that income after your death in order to provide for your family’s basic living expenses.

The conventional wisdom in the insurance industry is that you should maintain a life insurance policy equal to between 10 times and 20 times your annual income. So if you earn around $50K per year, that would mean policy coverage between $500K and $1 million.

The complication today is that with interest rates being as low as they are that might not be enough either.

For example, if you have a $1 million policy that could be invested at 5% per year, your family could live on the interest earned – which conveniently comes to $50,000 per year – for the next 20 years.

That would still leave the original $1 million intact to cover other expenses. But with today’s microscopic interest rates, there’s no way to get a guaranteed return of 5% on your money, certainly not for 15 or 20 years.

Also, keep in mind that most insurance companies have a maximum multiplier you can apply to your income for life insurance coverage. For example, it wouldn’t make much sense for a 22-year-old making $27,000 per year to get a $2 million life insurance. Or a 65-year-old that is retired to secure a $3 million dollar policy.

The table below is approximately how much you’re allowed to multiply your income based on your age and income:

Using the table above as a guide, a 35-year-old making $150,000 per year would be capped at taking out a $4.5 million term policy ($150,000 x 30 = $4,500,000).

Here we start with the basics – wrapping up your final affairs.

This will include funeral costs and any lingering medical costs. A reasonable estimate for a typical funeral is around $20,000.

Crazy, right? You can get burial insurance to cover only the most basic of final expenses.

Debt burdens are high in the US, and debt can be especially crushing on remaining family members. Many life insurance customers make sure they can pay off most of their debt with the policy.

Medical costs are a serious variable. Even if you have excellent health insurance, there are likely to be unpaid medical bills lingering after your death. This has to do with copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance provisions.

Collectively, they can add up to many thousands of dollars. But where things get really complicated is if you die of a terminal illness.

For example, if you are stricken by an illness that lasts for several years, you could incur a number of expenses that are not covered by insurance. This may include the cost of personal care and even experimental treatments.

A home may be a large asset, but it’s also often a homeowner’s largest debt. The average mortgage balance in the US is roughly $236,443 according to Experian data. So you could easily use a life insurance policy to pay off that debt and relieve your loved ones of a monthly mortgage payment.

Credit card debt and other personal debt are some of the most expensive obligations carrying rates upward of 20% in some cases. Make sure you have enough to cover this very expensive debt.

Below is a sampling of major expenses your family is likely to incur, either on an annual basis or at some point after your death.

Tuition costs continue to skyrocket. The Department of Education suggests that four-year public college tuition has been rising an average of 5% per year, far exceeding the rate of inflation. If you have one child who attends an in-state public school, a second at an out-of-state public school, and a third in a private university, the total expenditure will reach $416,560.

Vehicles and other forms of transportation represent another large sum. Unfortunately, with increasing electronics and safety features, the average cost of a new car continues to grow.

If your family relies on your work for healthcare, take notice. According to eHealth.com, the average health insurance premium for a family is $22,221. That’s a shade under $2,000 per month in additional cost. This cost will only rise, and the need could last for years.

So far, we’ve been describing the financial obligations likely to affect a typical household.But there may be certain situations that will produce obligations that are less obvious.

For example, if you’re a business owner, there may be debts or other financial obligations that will need to be paid upon your death.

Even though no one in your family may be qualified or interested in taking over your business, the payoff of those obligations may be completely necessary to enable the sale of the business.

Another possibility is that you’re a real estate investor.

If your properties are heavily indebted, extra insurance proceeds may be necessary either to carry the properties until they’re sold, or even to pay off existing indebtedness to free up cash flow for income.

You may even need additional funds if you are taking care of an extended family member, like an aging parent.

These are just some of the many possibilities of expenses that will need to be covered by insurance proceeds.

Before we move on to specific life insurance quotes, let’s first consider the factors that affect term life insurance premiums.

This is typically the single most important premium factor. The older you are, the more likely you are to die within the term of the policy.

This is a close second and why it’s so important to apply for a policy as early in life as possible. Premiums on life insurances rates literally increase by each year.

If you have any health conditions that may affect mortality, such as diabetes or hypertension, your premiums will be higher. This is another compelling reason to apply while you are young and in good health.

It’s not that policies are not available to people with health conditions, it’s just that they’re less expensive if you don’t have any.

A 10-year term policy will have a lower premium than a 20-year term policy, which will be lower than a 30-year term. The shorter the term, the less likely it is the insurance company will have to pay a claim before it expires.

Size of the policy matters, but not the way you might think. Yes, a $1 million policy will cost more than a $500,000 policy. But it won’t cost twice as much.

The larger the policy, the lower the per-thousand cost will be.

When the size of the death benefit is considered, the larger policy will always be more cost-effective.

For example, certain occupations are more hazardous than others (think policeman versus librarian). Deep-sea diving is higher risk than golf. And smoking is the one activity guaranteed to raise your premiums substantially.

With this information in mind, let’s take a look at whether you should consider a $1 million whole life policy instead.

Any discussion on life insurance should include a comparison of whole life and term life insurance coverage. After all, both products can be immensely valuable in the right situation, yet one product (whole life) costs considerably more than the other.

Most of the time, the debate is settled in favor of term life insurance based on cost alone.

A whole life insurance policy can easily cost 10x the same amount of coverage you can get with a term policy.

With that being said, whole life insurance and other investment-type life insurance coverage can be valuable in terms of the cash value you can build up over time. Whole life insurance also offers a fixed benefit amount for your heirs that will last for your entire life, yet the cost of your premiums are guaranteed to stay the same.

The cash value of a whole life insurance policy also grows on a tax-deferred basis, and you can borrow against this amount if you need a loan. Further, many whole life policies from reputable providers also pay out dividends during good years, which can be substantial.

The problem with whole life and other similar policies like universal life is the fact that premiums can be exorbitant for the amount of coverage you might need.

A couple with young children provides a good example since they might need a $1 million dollar policy or more to provide income protection for their working years and have money left for college tuition and other expenses.

With young families, expenses are already high.

This includes costs for food for a family, childcare, heavy use of health care, and the seemingly endless demand for clothing, furniture, and even entertainment as the children grow.

As you can see from the cost comparison below from State Farm, there’s not enough room in the typical family budget to afford the type of life insurance that’s needed.

A 40-year-old mother and breadwinner in excellent health would pay $80.09 per month for a term life policy that lasts 20 years, whereas a whole life policy in the same amount would cost $1,266.69 per month (or $14,560 annually).

This is a classic situation where term insurance rides to the rescue. The family can afford to buy the amount of coverage they need at an affordable price, whereas paying for permanent life insurance coverage in the same amount would be difficult to justify.

And just as important for people of any age and in any circumstance, the extra funds not being spent on insurance premiums can be invested to gradually improve your financial situation.

So absolutely, term insurance will work best for most people.

As you’ll notice, each table has a wide array of information. Knowing that everybody is in a different situation, I wanted to make sure that I offered term life quotes for almost every conceivable situation.

I’ve included life insurance rates for a 30-year term, 20-year term, and a 10-year term million dollar life policies. If you’re a tobacco user, I’ve also included some quotes from life insurance for smokers.

For those that think that a million-dollar term policy is expensive, you’ll quickly notice that a 25-year-old male in good health only costs $645 per year while a 35-year-old costs $795.

On a monthly basis that’s almost next to nothing!

There is a big drop-off in life insurance rates between a 20 year and a 30 year since underwriters do not have to worry as much about life expectancy.

For many people, a 20-year policy gets them exactly where they want to be in life when the policy term runs out.

If you’ve made the decision that $1 million of life insurance is the right amount of coverage you need and you’re ready to purchase a policy, here are the steps you’ll need to follow.

1. Determine How Much Coverage You Need: This is the first and most important step in securing a million life insurance policies. You need to have a clear understanding of how much coverage you actually need.

2. Choose the Right Type of Policy: There are whole life, term life, and Universal life policies available. Choose the one that best suits your needs.

3. Shop Around: Don’t just go with the first life insurance company you come across. It’s important to compare life insurance rates and coverage from a few different companies before making a decision.

4. Consider Your Health: If you’re in good health, you’ll likely qualify for lower rates. However, if you have health issues, you may still be able to get coverage, but it will probably be more expensive.

5. Consider Your Lifestyle: If you have a risky job or hobby, that could affect your rates.

6. Get Quotes From Multiple Companies: This is the best way to compare rates and find the cheapest policy.

7. Read the Fine Print: Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions of the policy before buying it.

8. Buy Online: You can usually get cheaper rates by buying life insurance online.

9. Pay Attention to Your Payment Schedule: Most life insurance policies require monthly or annual payments. Be sure you can afford the payments before buying a policy.

10. Review Your Policy Regularly: Life changes, and so do life insurance needs. Be sure to review your policy regularly to make sure it still meets your needs.

Following these steps will help you get the best possible rate on a million-dollar life insurance policy.

Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing on the dotted line. Also, make sure to shop around and compare rates from multiple companies before buying a policy.

A $1 million term life insurance policy is a type of life insurance that provides coverage for a specific period of time, usually 10-20 years. If you die during the term of the policy, your beneficiaries will receive a death benefit of $1 million. If you live past the term of the policy, the policy will expire and you will not receive any death benefit. A $1 million term life insurance policy is a good choice for people who want to make sure their loved ones are taken care of financially if something happens to them. It can also be a good choice for people with a lot of debt, like a mortgage or student loans, that they want to make sure is paid off if they die.

A million-dollar life insurance policy can give you and your loved one’s peace of mind knowing that they will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

#8636. What Are Mutual Funds?

Some products in this article are from our partners. Read our Advertiser Discloser.

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

Each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund company or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most important things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

For most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

When you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly

This is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

With thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

That said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most important step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.
