Are you trying to win the Mega Millions, but your numbers never seem to come up? It may be time to look for better ways to make money. Fortunately, you can earn extra cash without going and getting a “real job.”

What are the best ways to avoid sitting in a cubicle all day? Some money-making strategies require an upfront investment, while others let you earn money in your free time with the help of apps.

Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

One of the easiest ways to earn money is by signing up to participate in market research studies. You won’t make much, a few dollars here and there, but you can create a free account and get started within minutes.

You’ll be paid in PayPal cash or gift cards for sharing your opinion and completing other tasks online.

E-Poll Market Research is one of the top companies to consider for this type of work. They make it easy to create an account and answer survey questions.

However, there are plenty of other options to consider, including:

While market research gigs won’t make you rich, it’s something you can do during your spare time.

If you have a book idea, turning your story into an eBook can help you earn passive income without a regular job. Kindle Direct Publishing can even help you format your book for Kindle, at which point you can market and sell your book to millions of potential readers who shop on Amazon.com.

How much can you earn writing eBooks? That depends on how many books you write, how much you sell them for, and how successful you are at marketing your book. Selling 20 books per month with a profit of $7 per book would net you $140 per month and $1,680 per year.

Meanwhile, selling 100 books per month at $7 per book would net you $700 per month and $8,400 per year. Need a little inspiration? Here’s an article that shows you how to make your first $1,000 selling eBooks.

You can earn a lot of money by starting a blog or niche website and monetizing it. I should know. I started Good Financial Cents more than a decade ago, and have earned millions of dollars through the monetization of this site since its earliest days.

How do you make money blogging? Earning real income with a website isn’t as easy as it looks, but there are plenty of monetization strategies you can try.

Here are the most common ways blogs make money:

If you’re curious about what it takes to earn money blogging, consider signing up for my Make 1K Challenge. It’s free and can help you earn your first $1,000 online with some of the blog monetization strategies I’ve already mentioned.

You could argue that freelance work is like a regular job, but working at home and on your terms is much different from traditional employment. The fact is, most freelancers are fully remote – they can work from anywhere in the world with a laptop and an internet connection.

Plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

Of course, you’ll need a marketable skill to find paid work as a freelancer. This could be freelance writing, design skills, marketing expertise, or something else.

You can use several websites to market your skills as a freelancer, including:

HealthyWage makes it possible to earn money while you lose weight. You won’t earn a ton of cash through the app, but you can earn a few dollars and use it to supplement other income you have.

The more weight you lose, the more money you can make. For example, the HealthyWage website claims some of their clients who lost more than 100 pounds managed to earn anywhere from $1,400 to $3,000.

However, the HW weight loss calculator shows potential earnings of $578 to $828 for people who only have 15 pounds to lose.

If you have a car you rarely use and want to earn some side income, you can consider renting it out with Turo, a ride-sharing platform that connects car owners with people who need a short-term rental. You can set your price, although you’ll have more success if you price your car competitively.

Nicer vehicles in high-demand areas can easily fetch rates that surpass $100 per day through this platform. Turo notes that in-demand cars rented out regularly can bring in anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 per year in net profit.

Plus, almost anyone can rent out their car provided it meets the guidelines of the Turo platform. Your car must be 12 years old or newer with less than 130,000 miles. It must be worth less than $200,000 (no Lambo’s), and you must also meet Turo’s auto insurance requirements.

Do you have a spare bedroom in your home that you never use? Maybe you have a basement or garage apartment you could fix up and begin renting for a profit?

Either way, Airbnb lets you rent out rooms and other spaces in your home on any dates you prefer. You must let renters know they’re renting a room in a home vs. an entire apartment or house and provide as much additional detail as possible.

The amount you can earn will depend on where you live and the type of accommodation you can offer. However, expensive cities like Chicago, New York, and San Francisco have plenty of rooms for rent that go for well over $100 per night.

You may not have an entire room you can rent, but even if you have some storage space, Neighbor.com allows you to rent it out to others in need.

Common spaces rented through this platform include

The Neighbor.com platform makes it easy to advertise your unused space so that people nearby can inquire if they’re interested. Also, note that the platform offers insurance that can protect you if some of your client’s items are damaged or stolen while in your care.

How much can you make renting out extra space? It depends on how much space you have to rent and where it’s located. However, Neighbor.com shows a range of rental space options that cost anywhere from $20 to $100+ per month.

Investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

But what exactly is a dividend stock? For the most part, they are regular stocks but with a track record of sharing their profits with investors through dividends.

Dividends can also be earned in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds, and they can be significant once you build up a large portfolio.

Since dividends are paid by profitable companies, they tend to be seen as less risky for investors. If you’re curious about what it takes to get started with this strategy, this post explains how to invest in dividend stocks.

Housesitting is an option if you’re somewhat mobile and can move from place to place. Generally, you can find house-sitting gigs through word of mouth, referrals, or online portals like Craigslist.org or Facebook Marketplace.

That said, not all house-sitting gigs are paid. Some offer the potential for exotic travel instead and free lodging for a week to several months.

Either way, a website called TrustedHousesitters is the best place to find house-sitting gigs. Some jobs posted are for house-sitting only, while others require house sitters to provide basic care for pets or plants.

If you have serious wanderlust and want to travel far and wide, this platform can help make it happen. Many gigs posted online are in countries like Australia, Ireland, France, and Switzerland.

If you love animals and want to earn money taking care of them, several platforms can help turn your dream into a reality.

For example, Rover.com lets you provide basic care for dogs or cats in your home, or you can pick up dog walking gigs. Another mobile app, called Wag!, lets you do more of the same.

You can set your rates for all types of work through these platforms, and your availability. While earnings vary by location and job, most people watch dogs and cats for anywhere from $40 to $100 per night.

Real estate investing may seem like a pipe dream if you hope to earn income without a job but hear me out. There are many ways to earn income through real estate without owning physical property or dealing with the hassles of being a landlord.

You can invest in real estate investment trusts (REITs) that let you build wealth over time. You can also use a platform called Fundrise to invest in real estate with a minimum investment of $10.

Fundrise lets you purchase eREITs, large investment funds that acquire, own, or operate multi-residential and commercial properties. The income you earn is entirely passive since it handles the work of finding income-producing properties and managing them.

While returns are never guaranteed, Fundrise investors have achieved very solid returns. Investors who use the platform earned an average return of 7.31% in 2020, followed by 22.99% in 2021, 1.50% in 2022 and -7.45% in 2023 (their first down year).

You can earn income on your spare change by investing it using Acorns. The roundup savings app syncs to your debit or credit card rounds up every purchase you make to the nearest dollar, and invests the difference. Once it’s set up, there’s no work on your part.

Most of the money is invested in ETFs and managed by the world’s top investment firms like Vanguard and BlackRock. While this app makes it easy to invest small amounts of money, it’s not free to use. Personal plans start at $3 per month, while a family plan costs just $5.

If you’re looking for some paid gigs that are relatively easy, consider setting up a profile on TaskRabbit, an online platform that lets you get paid for completing various tasks, such as:

Projects typically pay between $30 and $100, although some pay significantly more than that. TaskRabbit also lets you pick and choose the jobs you want to take on based on your availability so that you can work entirely on your schedule.

If you love taking photographs and have a knack for getting professional-looking images, you can use your skills and expertise to sell photos online.

Websites like Depositphotos and iStockPhoto pay photographers to supply them with stock photos they can sell to writers, publications, and various online platforms.

The best part about this side hustle is that you can get started with the equipment you already have. While you can use a professional camera if you want to, many smartphones take professional-quality photos.

Earning a bank bonus is another way to earn money without a regular job, but you’ll need an upfront investment to get started. Most bonus offers require you to deposit a specific amount of money and keep it in your account for up to 12 months.

You may also be required to set up direct deposit to earn a bank bonus, and other terms and conditions may apply.

Where can you find the best bank bonuses? While bonus offers constantly change, you can start by checking with banks like Chase, HSBC, Radius Bank, and Wells Fargo.

Flipping furniture requires some upfront legwork and potentially even some artistic talent, but you can earn a solid income with this strategy if you know what you’re doing.

Essentially, this side hustle requires you to shop at thrift stores, garage sales, and online platforms to find furniture that will ultimately sell for more than you paid.

From there, you can sell the furniture as-is or clean it up and paint it with the goal of fetching an even higher price.

You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

If you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

Starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

That said, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

Donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

That said, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

If you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, update a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

Another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

Unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

Finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

You won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

Other online survey sites to check out include the following:

With all this being said, you’ll want to keep in mind that most surveys only pay a few bucks and that some only pay you with gift cards, while others offer the option for PayPal transfers. Make sure you understand how each survey site works and how you get paid before you sign up.

There you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

Check out the video below if you’re looking for even more ways to make money.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing

Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you plan a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on or around the 1st of each month. Set a calendar reminder. Follow Flying Blue on social media and sign up for their email newsletter — they announce the month's featured routes there. The ChooseFI community forums and travel rewards deal-tracking sites will also surface these announcements within minutes of release.

When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Note: Flying Blue's search only shows Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

Do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move quickly through the next steps.

From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

With miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Let's walk through a redemption that the ChooseFI community has actually executed.

The Route: New York (JFK) → Paris (CDG) in Business class on Air France

The Cash Price: A direct Air France Business class ticket on this route typically retails between $3,000 and $5,500 depending on the season. For this example, let's use a realistic mid-range price of $3,800.

The Promo Reward Price: 40,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, plus approximately $60–$80 in taxes and fees. No fuel surcharges — because it's a Promo award.

The CPP Calculation: $3,800 ÷ 40,000 miles = 9.5 cents per point. That's nearly 10x what you'd get using those same Chase points for cash back at 1 cent each.

You board at JFK and step into Air France's Business class cabin — the same product that Business travelers are paying $3,800+ to access. You have a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, a curated French menu with Champagne service before takeoff, noise-canceling headphones, an amenity kit, and pajamas on longer segments. The CDG lounge is yours before departure — the Air France lounge in Terminal 2E is a genuine culinary experience, not an airport afterthought. You land in Paris rested, not wrecked.

For a couple, you'd need 80,000 miles total — both ways would be 160,000 miles. A pair of Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve cardholders who signed up in the same year could realistically have this banked between welcome bonuses and everyday spend. Transfer from Chase to Flying Blue: instant. Time from decision to booking: under 15 minutes.

You did not pay $7,600 for two Business class tickets across the Atlantic. You paid 80,000 points and roughly $160 in fees. Those points cost you, at most, $800 in credit card spend if you valued them at 1 cent each — meaning you captured $7,440 in travel value from an $800 equivalent investment in points. That's the FI multiplier that makes this program worth mastering.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st

Flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns

Promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can plan your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

The ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

It's hard because of **timing and availability** — two factors that reward the prepared and punish the passive. **What Specifically Makes This Hard:** 1. **Monthly availability windows are brief.** You have 24–48 hours from the Promo announcement to act before the best dates disappear. If you're not watching, you miss the cycle entirely and wait another month. 2. **Dynamic pricing outside of Promo is punishing.** If you miss the Promo window and try to book a standard award on the same route, you could pay 2–3x more miles. The program's value is almost entirely concentrated in the monthly Promo structure. 3. **Coordination across accounts takes discipline.** Keeping 40,000–80,000 points liquid in a transferable account, not spending them on something else, and being ready to move instantly requires real points discipline. **Three Tips to Overcome the Challenge:** - **Automate your awareness.** Sign up for Flying Blue emails and follow deal-tracking communities so the announcement comes to you. - **Keep your points liquid in Chase or Amex.** The instant transfer speeds are your competitive advantage over slower-moving transfer paths. - **Be route-flexible, not date-flexible.** You may not get Paris in July, but you might get Amsterdam in September — and that's still an extraordinary redemption. #8627. Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

Some products in this article are from our partners. Read our Advertiser Discloser.

If your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance company. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA plans, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health plan with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace plans are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing plan cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

#8625. Why The 401(k) Still Dominates (Even Its Inventor Has Doubts)

In 1980, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna figured out how to use Section 401(k), a little-known provision Congress added to the tax code in 1978, to build the first 401(k) plan. It quickly became a favorite among companies looking to offer employees more retirement benefits.

Today, it is still the cornerstone of retirement planning in America. Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first.

Recently, Benna has made headlines for calling out his invention, the 401(k), for disproportionately rewarding the wealthy. He may have a point. But I still think the 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

Also read: Beyond the 401(k): Why Physicians Are Turning to Defined Benefit Plans

In a recent Bloomberg interview, Benna argued that the modern 401(k) has grown too complicated and too costly, and that it benefits wealthier savers more than middle- and lower-income workers, the people who arguably need it most.

Affluent employees can afford to max out an account and reap the tax break on top. Benna believes low-income workers either lack access to a plan or can’t afford to contribute if they do.

Research seems to agree. Researchers at Vanguard, Yale and MIT found that about 44% of employer matching dollars go to the top 20% of earners at their companies.

And the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported that while 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution (DC) plan such as a 401(k), only 49% participate. That means roughly 3 in 10 workers who could use a plan but don’t.

Source: BLS. Alt text: BLS chart showing 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution plan and 49% participate, March 2026

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Most physicians sit on the other side of this. Every specialty earns well above the national average. Doximity’s latest compensation report names pediatric infectious disease as the lowest-paying specialty, at $217,819. By comparison, the average American salary is $69,770.

The reason I bring this up here is so that physicians who run practices can make sure their employee 401(k) structures do not reflect these statistics. More on that below.

The 401(k) has been one of the most effective tools for building middle-class wealth the U.S. has ever had.

Household stock ownership went up from 32% in 1989, right before one of the best multi-decade stretches for stock returns on record, to 58% by 2022. Almost one-fifth of American households now hold a net worth above a million dollars— much of it held in home equity and retirement accounts like the 401(k)..

So even if the account rewards people who already earn enough to contribute, it still enables actual wealth-building for millions of ordinary workers who’d otherwise have little beyond Social Security waiting for them at retirement.

Access and participation are both on the rise largely thanks to policy changes. Many states now require employers without a retirement plan to enroll workers in a state-run IRA program. Employers can usually opt out by setting up their own plan, which is pushing more of them to offer a 401(k).

Small businesses, which employ close to half the American workforce, have historically skipped retirement benefits altogether. Tax credits and cheaper providers are changing that. Cerulli Associates projects that the number of 401(k) plans will grow 36% over the next five years, passing one million by the end of the decade.

Auto-enrollment deserves a lot of the credit for the jump in participation.

Under SECURE 2.0, 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after December 29, 2022 must automatically enroll employees, starting with plan years that began in 2025. Older plans, businesses less than three years old and employers with 10 or fewer workers are exempt.

The effect is large. Vanguard found that plans with auto-enrollment had a 94% participation rate, compared with 64% for plans where employees sign up on their own.

Learn more: Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

For 2026, the IRS raised the 401(k) employee contribution limit to $24,500, up from $23,500 in 2025. Workers 50 and older can add a catch-up contribution of $8,000 on top of that, up from $7,500, bringing the total to $32,500 for savers in that age bracket.

A newer “super” catch-up of $11,250 lets savers ages 60 to 63 put away even more. It replaces the regular $8,000 catch-up for those years rather than stacking on top of it, bringing their total to $35,750.

re limited to 72,000for2026(80,000 with the age-50 catch-up, or $83,250 for ages 60 to 63), or 100% of eligible pay, whichever is lower. If your plan allows after-tax contributions, the room between your own contributions and that cap is what makes a mega backdoor Roth possible.

Important: starting in 2026, if your wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000 in 2025, any catch-up contributions you make must go in as Roth (after-tax) instead of pretax. Two details matter for physicians:

If you’re weighing Roth against pretax for the rest of your contributions, here’s how to choose between a Roth and traditional 401(k). Full details are on the IRS catch-up contributions page.

Many employed physicians don’t have a 401(k) at all. Hospitals and academic centers usually offer a 403(b), which works almost the same way, with the same $24,500 limit and the same catch-ups.

Many also offer a 457(b), which has its own separate $24,500 limit. If you have both, you can defer up to $49,000 in 2026 before counting any catch-ups.

One caution: in a non-governmental 457(b), the money technically belongs to your employer until it’s paid out, so it’s exposed if the hospital runs into financial trouble. Here’s our full guide to 457(b) contributions.

If you own a practice with staff, plan design decides who actually benefits. A safe harbor 401(k) is the common choice. You make a required contribution for employees, either 3% of pay or a match of up to 4%, which vests right away.

In return, the plan skips the annual nondiscrimination tests that can otherwise cap what owners contribute. Under SECURE 2.0, small practices can also claim tax credits of up to $5,000 a year for three years toward startup costs, plus $500 a year for adding auto-enrollment.

Owners who want to save more than the 401(k) allows often pair it with a cash balance plan. And if you’re a solo practitioner with no staff, a solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA is usually simpler.

More than 80% of employers who sponsor a 401(k) offer some form of match, usually tied to how much the employee contributes. Some employers match dollar for dollar up to a set percentage of salary.

Others match 50 cents on the dollar up to a higher contribution threshold. The formula changes how much match each dollar you contribute actually earns, and that’s where dual-income households can come out ahead.

A brief published by the Center for Retirement Research (CRR) examined whether married couples coordinate contributions to capture both employer matches. Just over 40% of couples actively coordinate to maximize their combined match and roughly one in five couples leaves match money uncaptured.

In one example from the brief, a couple decides how to split $480 a month in savings between two accounts with different match formulas. Moving contributions toward the partner with the more generous 1-to-1 match, as opposed to splitting evenly, nets the household an extra $30 a month in employer money.

Stretched over 30 years at a 5% inflation-adjusted return, that $30 monthly difference compounds into roughly $25,000 in additional retirement savings, without either partner setting aside a single extra dollar of their own income.

Source: CRR. Alt text: CRR chart showing how couples split 401(k) contributions to capture employer matches.

Plenty of couples capture both matches without planning it, because each partner contributes enough on their own. That works fine.

Coordination matters when money is tight, like when one spouse is still in residency, working part-time or paying down loans hard. In those years, send your savings to the richer match first, then fill the other.

Say a resident earning $66,000 and her spouse earning $120,000 can save $600 a month between them. Her plan matches 50 cents per dollar on the first 6% of pay. His matches dollar for dollar on the first 4%, up to $400 a month.

Split evenly at $300 each, they collect $450 a month in match. If he puts in $400 and she puts in $200, they collect $500. That’s an extra $600 a year in employer money from the same $600 a month.

Compare match formulas with your spouse, figure out which account pays the better rate, and adjust the split.

Finally, if you’re wondering about how aggressively you should contribute, I’ll say that starting early beats chasing a better return.

In an example from Forbes, we see two 25-year-old savers earning identical salaries. One enrolls immediately at a 10% deferral rate with a 3% match. The other waits five years, then contributes 6% to capture the same 3% match.

The second saver’s fund even outperforms the first, returning roughly 8.9% annually versus 8.4%, partly from a private equity allocation meant to make up lost ground.

By 65, the early starter still ends up with roughly $3 million, compared with $2 million for the saver who waited. That $1 million gap comes from two things: five fewer years of compounding and a lower savings rate (9% of pay versus 13%). The higher return didn’t come close to closing it. If you’re still in training, here’s what to set up now.

As you can see, when it comes to retirement savings, your timing often matters more than any other variable.

A dollar contributed at 25 has decades to compound and no later contribution, however large, can fully make up for a late start. The 401(k) is also one of the few accounts you can start on day one without worrying much about what happens when you change jobs.

That’s because, as opposed to pensions and employer-funded bonus plans, the 401(k) is portable. Your own contributions are yours the moment they hit your account, and they go with you when you leave. Employer matches can be different. Many plans vest the match over time, either all at once after up to three years or gradually over up to six.

Leave before you’re vested and you lose the unvested part, so check your plan’s vesting schedule before you time a job change. You can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA, and it will continue to compound without interruption.

Benna may not be happy with how his invention turned out, but for me, looking at how it has created a new class of millionaires, it is the one non-negotiable account in retirement planning for physicians and beyond.

Yes. A 401(k) invests in the market through mutual funds or target-date funds, so balances can drop during downturns. Over decades, though, contributions and compounding have historically outpaced short-term losses for most savers.

It depends. A 401(k) is portable, so you keep the balance and can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA when you switch jobs. A pension pays guaranteed income for life, but most of the benefit builds in your later years with one employer, so people who change jobs often come out behind.

#8624. Solo Health Review (2026): Costs, Coverage, Pros & Cons

If you’re self-employed, finding affordable health coverage can be challenging. Traditional health insurance premiums can take a big bite out of your budget, especially when you’re paying for coverage without employer help.

Solo Health offers a different approach to health coverage designed specifically for entrepreneurs, freelancers, and self-employed business owners. Instead of purchasing a traditional individual health insurance policy, eligible business owners establish a self-funded major medical plan through their business.

But how does Solo Health work? Is the coverage comprehensive? And could it actually save you money? In this Solo Health review, we’ll break down the costs, benefits, potential drawbacks, and important details you should understand before enrolling.

Solo Health is a health coverage solution designed for self-employed individuals and business owners who want an alternative to traditional individual health insurance.

The company offers self-funded major medical plans that provide access to healthcare services through a nationwide PPO provider network.

Unlike a traditional insurance policy purchased through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace, Solo Health uses a business-based structure.

Your business establishes its own self-funded health plan to cover eligible medical claims.

According to Solo Health, its plans include:

One of Solo Health’s biggest selling points is major medical coverage specifically designed for self-employed people.

However, Solo Health is not a traditional ACA Marketplace insurance policy, and eligibility depends on a health questionnaire.

Solo Health operates differently from both traditional health insurance and healthcare-sharing programs. Instead of purchasing an individual insurance policy, your business establishes a self-funded health plan.

That self-funded plan pays eligible medical claims under the terms of your plan documents.

Here’s a simplified overview of how it works:

Preventive care is generally covered without meeting your deductible.

Prescription medications have their own coverage rules, including copays after the deductible.

Solo Health describes its product as a self-funded major medical health plan, not a healthcare-sharing ministry or a conventional individual insurance policy.

Eligible medical claims are paid through your business’s self-funded health plan.

While Solo Health provides major medical benefits, you should not assume it has all the same eligibility protections, regulatory requirements, or consumer safeguards as an ACA-compliant individual insurance policy.

For example, Solo Health requires applicants to complete a health questionnaire and meet its participation requirements. This differs significantly from ACA Marketplace plans, which generally cannot reject applicants because of preexisting medical conditions.

Before enrolling, make sure you understand the plan documents, coverage exclusions, and how the plan pays medical claims.

Solo Health offers several key medical benefits designed to protect members from both routine healthcare expenses and larger medical bills.

Here’s a closer look at what is included.

Solo Health covers eligible preventive healthcare services at 100%, with no deductible required.

This can be particularly helpful for self-employed individuals who want to stay on top of their health without paying the full cost of every preventive appointment. However, diagnostic tests or treatments performed during a preventive visit may be billed differently.

Solo Health covers primary care physicians and medical specialists. Members can access participating providers through the MultiPlan PHCS network, now associated with Claritev.

You generally don’t need a referral to see a specialist. For most non-preventive visits, you’ll pay the applicable cost until you meet your deductible. After you meet your deductible, the plan covers eligible medical services at 100%, subject to plan terms.

One of the most important reasons to have health coverage is protection against unexpected medical emergencies. A serious accident, hospitalization, or surgery can result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills.

According to the company, emergency services are processed as in-network regardless of which hospital provides the care.

Certain planned hospital admissions and surgeries require prior authorization.

Solo Health covers eligible mental health and substance use treatment. This can include outpatient therapy and other qualifying services. However, limits apply.

For example, Solo Health limits outpatient mental health therapy to 40 visits per covered individual each year. Some mental health treatments may also require prior authorization. If you regularly use mental health services, review these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health includes prescription benefits administered through FairosRx. Preventive medications in Tier 1 are covered at $0. For other covered medications, members generally pay the discounted cost until they meet their deductible.

Afterward, prescription copays apply based on the medication’s tier. Some specialty medications can still involve high out-of-pocket costs.

Solo Health also lists maternity and newborn care among its covered benefits. This can include eligible prenatal services, childbirth, and medical care for newborns.

However, anyone planning to start or expand a family should review the plan’s maternity provisions, eligibility requirements, and applicable exclusions before enrolling. Don’t assume every pregnancy-related service will automatically qualify for payment.

One of the biggest questions when considering any health coverage option is how much you’ll pay. Solo Health offers three plan designs, each with a different deductible.

The main difference between these plans is how much you must pay toward eligible medical expenses before the plan pays most covered costs at 100%.

All three plans offer the same core coverage and provider network. The deductible you select influences your monthly payment. Generally speaking, plans with lower deductibles cost more per month, while plans with higher deductibles cost less.

Your actual monthly cost depends on factors such as your age, location, household composition, and eligibility. Because pricing is individualized, the best way to determine your cost is to request a quote directly from Solo Health.

Let’s say you choose the Solo Health plan with a $5,000 individual deductible. You would generally pay the applicable cost of eligible non-preventive healthcare services until you’ve spent $5,000 toward your deductible.

After that, the plan pays 100% of eligible medical expenses for the remainder of the plan year. However, prescription copays and potential out-of-network charges can still apply.

This is why it’s important to understand the difference between your deductible and your total possible healthcare expenses.

Solo Health advertises its deductible as the out-of-pocket maximum for eligible medical care.

This structure can make medical expenses easier to plan for.

However, the advertised maximum may not cover every expense you could incur.

Prescription copays, excluded services, and charges above the plan’s out-of-network reimbursement amount may result in additional costs.

When comparing plans, consider both your monthly payments and what you could reasonably afford if you had a major medical event.

Solo Health uses a six-tier prescription drug structure. Here is the company’s published schedule for covered medications after meeting the deductible.

Tier 1 preventive medications are available without meeting the deductible. For most other covered prescriptions, these copays apply after the deductible is satisfied. The plan also restricts certain expensive medications.

For example, the plan may exclude non-specialty medications that exceed specified price thresholds. If you take prescription medications regularly, check the company’s formulary to confirm whether your medications are covered and what they might cost.

A Health Savings Account (HSA) can be a valuable tool for managing healthcare expenses. HSAs can offer tax advantages when you contribute, invest, and use the funds for qualified medical expenses.

According to Solo Health’s published FAQ, the V2500 and V5000 plan designs are HSA-eligible, while the V10000 plan is not currently listed as HSA-eligible. However, HSA eligibility depends on federal tax requirements, not simply a plan’s marketing designation.

Before contributing, confirm that your specific coverage qualifies as an HSA-compatible high-deductible health plan under current IRS rules. This matters because deductible amounts alone don’t establish HSA eligibility.

Customer experiences can provide valuable insight when evaluating a healthcare company. However, a company’s advertised benefits differ from what customers experience when submitting medical claims.

Solo Health publishes information about its coverage, member services, and claims administration. It also offers concierge assistance and an online member portal.

Solo Health offers several features that may appeal to certain self-employed individuals.

Many freelancers and small business owners don’t have access to employer-sponsored health insurance. Solo Health is specifically designed for people in this situation.

Its business-based structure gives qualifying entrepreneurs another option to consider when shopping for health coverage.

Three deductible levels let members choose a plan that fits their financial situation. Someone with a larger emergency fund might prefer a higher deductible to reduce monthly costs.

Another person might prefer paying more each month in exchange for a lower deductible. The key is choosing a plan that fits both your budget and your ability to handle unexpected medical expenses.

Solo Health provides access to the MultiPlan PHCS network, which includes participating providers across all 50 states.

This may be especially valuable for entrepreneurs who travel frequently or work in multiple locations. Members can also seek out-of-network care, although additional financial risks can apply.

Unlike limited-benefit programs, Solo Health advertises coverage for major medical expenses such as hospital stays, surgeries, and emergency care.

It also includes preventive care, prescription benefits, and mental health services. The company states that there are no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits.

Solo Health’s business-based structure may offer tax advantages for eligible business owners. The company states that monthly plan costs are generally deductible as a business expense.

However, the tax treatment depends on your business structure and individual circumstances. Consult a qualified tax professional before assuming your payments will qualify for a deduction.

Eligible preventive services are covered at 100% from the beginning of coverage. This feature helps people prioritize preventive care while managing overall medical expenses.

While Solo Health has appealing features, it also has important limitations.

Solo Health requires applicants to have an eligible business with an active EIN. Applicants must also complete a health questionnaire.

If you don’t meet the company’s participation requirements, you may not qualify for coverage. This makes Solo Health less accessible than ACA Marketplace coverage, which generally offers guaranteed issue during applicable enrollment periods.

A $10,000 deductible may be manageable for someone with substantial savings. However, it could create financial hardship for someone living paycheck to paycheck.

Before selecting a high-deductible plan, make sure you have enough savings to handle unexpected healthcare costs. The lowest monthly payment isn’t necessarily the best financial decision if it exposes you to expenses you cannot afford.

Solo Health uses reference-based pricing for out-of-network services. This means the plan may reimburse a benchmarked amount rather than the provider’s full billed charge.

If the provider charges more than the plan allows, you could be responsible for the difference. This is sometimes called balance billing.

Although Solo Health offers support services to help members navigate medical bills, that does not necessarily eliminate the risk of additional charges.

Solo Health’s enrollment process includes health-related eligibility questions. This differs from ACA-compliant individual health insurance.

If you have ongoing medical conditions or a complicated medical history, review the eligibility requirements carefully.

Accurate answers are essential, and the company states that incomplete or inaccurate information can result in denial of coverage.

Although Solo Health advertises no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits, certain services have visit limits.

For example, outpatient mental health therapy is generally limited to 40 visits annually per covered individual. Some treatments also require prior authorization. Read the complete plan documents so you understand these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health’s self-funded model may be unfamiliar to people who have only purchased traditional insurance.

The arrangement involves a self-funded business health plan, third-party administration, and a medical reimbursement policy.

Because this structure differs from a standard individual insurance policy, it is worth reviewing the legal and financial responsibilities involved.

How does Solo Health compare with a conventional ACA Marketplace plan?

Traditional ACA Marketplace insurance offers important consumer protections, including guaranteed coverage of preexisting conditions and standardized requirements for essential health benefits.

Solo Health offers a different structure that may appeal to qualifying business owners. However, these products are not interchangeable. For someone with ongoing medical needs, ACA-compliant coverage may provide greater predictability around eligibility and consumer protections.

For an eligible entrepreneur, Solo Health may be worth comparing based on its benefits, provider access, and total annual costs.

Another useful comparison is Solo Health versus healthcare-sharing organizations such as Zion HealthShare. Although both may appeal to people exploring alternatives to conventional individual insurance, they work differently.

Solo Health offers a self-funded major medical plan established through an eligible business.

Its structure includes formal plan documents, medical claims administration, and a self-funded plan structure.

Zion HealthShare is a healthcare-sharing organization. Members contribute monthly amounts to share eligible medical expenses within the community.

Healthcare-sharing programs are not insurance, and they don’t guarantee payment of medical expenses the same way an insurance contract does.

The better option depends on your needs. Solo Health may be more appealing to business owners who want a structured major medical plan with a nationwide provider network.

Zion HealthShare may appeal to people who are comfortable with the healthcare-sharing model and its guidelines. Don’t choose either based on monthly costs alone. Consider the eligibility requirements, exclusions, payment structure, and your financial exposure if you experience a major medical event.

It may be particularly appealing to someone who wants to explore a business-based health plan rather than purchasing coverage through the individual insurance market.

If you have significant ongoing medical expenses, compare your options carefully.

Solo Health operates a business-based, self-funded major medical plan with a defined administrative structure. However, a documented plan structure does not independently verify financial strength, claims performance, or customer satisfaction.

Prospective members should review the legal documents and verify the applicable entities and regulatory disclosures.

Solo Health offers an interesting alternative for self-employed individuals seeking major medical coverage outside the traditional individual insurance market. Its biggest advantages include multiple deductible options, access to a nationwide PPO network, preventive care benefits, and coverage for significant medical expenses.

For qualifying entrepreneurs, the business-based structure may also provide financial and tax-planning opportunities. However, there are important trade-offs. Applicants must meet health eligibility requirements, higher deductibles can create substantial out-of-pocket costs, and out-of-network billing can become complicated.

I recommend comparing Solo Health with at least two other coverage options before deciding. Look beyond the monthly payment and calculate what you might spend over an entire year, including deductibles, prescription costs, and potential out-of-network expenses.

The goal isn’t simply to find the cheapest health plan. It’s to find coverage that protects your health and your finances when you need it most. Eligible self-employed business owners may want to explore Solo Health.

If your Medicare Advantage plan is ending, you have a limited-time right to buy a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policy without being turned down or charged more for your health. Use it by returning to Original Medicare instead of joining another Advantage plan, and apply before your old plan ends so your coverage has no gap.

Your plan has to mail you a non-renewal notice at least 90 days before it ends, so by early October. In July 2026, one of the largest Medicare Advantage insurers told investors its 2027 plan exits would affect about 600,000 members.

Outside your one-time Medigap open enrollment window, federal rules let insurers ask about your health, then turn you down or charge more. A plan exit flips that. If your Advantage plan leaves Medicare or your area, or you move out of its service area, insurers must sell you a policy, cover pre-existing conditions, and can’t charge more because of your health.

The right covers Plan G if you became eligible for Medicare in 2020 or later, Plan F if earlier, but not Plan N. To claim it:

The right lasts until 63 days after your old plan ends, but applying late leaves a gap. Leaving Advantage by choice? Get approved for Medigap before you drop your plan.

Mutual of Omaha is a strong place to start. AM Best rates Mutual of Omaha Insurance Company A+ (Superior). Its online tool prices Plan G from your ZIP code, birth date, and sex, with no contact details required, and you can apply online. Couples leaving the same plan can each save with its household discount where it’s available, though the amount and rules vary by state. Our Mutual of Omaha review has sample quotes from three cities.

Get that quote the day your notice arrives, and since every Plan G pays the same benefits, compare it with Medicare.gov’s list for your ZIP code. Pass on this right, and in most states a later switch means answering health questions.

Having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

If you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That said, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:

No matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data shows the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

To save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

The next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment plans.

If you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment plans and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

Once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

Then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

It’s important to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as quickly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

Finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

How much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

Focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

In the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

#8620. Buy Medigap in Your Six-Month Window – Don’t Count on Fall Open Enrollment

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Apply for a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policy in the six months that start once you’re 65 or older and enrolled in Part B. In that one-time window, insurers can’t turn you down or charge more because of your health. In most states, Medicare’s fall open enrollment offers no second chance, so don’t wait for it.

Once your six months end, insurers can ask about your health, then turn you down or charge more, unless a guaranteed-issue right applies. Major insurers’ applications list even high blood pressure as possible grounds for denial, a KFF review found. Only Connecticut and New York give everyone 65 and older another chance year-round. Massachusetts guarantees one every February and March, and Maine once a year for Plan A.

Two different periods are called open enrollment. Your six months are the Medigap Open Enrollment Period. Medicare’s fall open enrollment, Oct. 15 to Dec. 7, is for joining, switching, or dropping Medicare Advantage and drug plans, and only Rhode Island and Minnesota tie limited Medigap windows to it. State birthday rules don’t help first-time buyers either, since they only let people who already have Medigap switch plans.

If you work past 65, the window opens when Part B starts, even while you have a job-based plan, and can close before you need Medigap. When that plan pays before Medicare, as it does at employers with 20 or more workers, you can delay Part B without a late penalty and save the window for when the coverage ends. Helping a parent? Their Medicare card lists the Part B start date under MEDICAL.

Losing a Medicare Advantage plan brings a separate right, covered in our guide to Medigap after an Advantage plan ends.

Mutual of Omaha is a strong place to apply. Mutual of Omaha Insurance Company holds an A+ (Superior) financial strength rating from AM Best. Its online tool prices Plan G from your ZIP code, birth date, and sex, no contact details needed, and you can apply online. Couples can save with its household discount where it’s available, though the amount and rules vary by state.

Our Mutual of Omaha review has sample quotes from three cities. Plan G benefits don’t vary by insurer, so compare your quote with Medicare.gov’s Plan G prices for your ZIP code, then apply while your window is open.

#8619. Original Medicare Has No Out-of-Pocket Limit – Add One Before You Need Care

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Original Medicare puts no yearly limit on your out-of-pocket costs. Cap them with a Medigap policy like Plan G or a Medicare Advantage plan. If you choose Medigap, buy it in your six-month open enrollment window, when insurers can’t turn you down or charge more for your health.

Millions go without either one. KFF found that in 2023, 3.5 million people, 13% of everyone in traditional Medicare, lacked any supplemental coverage.

Without it, your share of Part B care is usually 20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the $283 deductible. By our math, a $100,000 year of outpatient cancer treatment leaves you more than $20,000 to pay. Part A adds a $1,736 hospital deductible in 2026 that you can owe more than once a year, plus daily charges for long hospital and skilled nursing stays.

Your Medigap window opens the first month you’re 65 or older with Part B, and it never repeats. Outside it, insurers in most states can ask health questions, then turn you down or charge more, unless a guaranteed issue right applies, such as your Advantage plan pulling out of your area.

To price Medigap, start with Mutual of Omaha. AM Best rates Mutual of Omaha Insurance Company A+ (Superior). Its online tool quotes Plan G and High-Deductible Plan G from your ZIP code, birth date, and sex, without asking for contact details. On Sept. 23, 2026, it quoted High-Deductible Plan G at $45.84 to $52.19 a month for a 65-year-old woman in Dallas (75201), Columbus (43215), and Phoenix (85004). Couples can save with its household discount where it’s available, though the amount and rules vary by state.

Plan G covers the same benefits at every insurer, so compare your Mutual of Omaha quote with Medicare.gov’s list for your ZIP code before you apply.
